title: Warm-up: 1 + 1 = 2
plain: A test problem for checking the submission pipeline. Prove that 1 + 1 = 2.
math: Prove $1+1=2$ in $\mathbb{N}$.

title: Minimal degree of a Jacobian counterexample
credit: Jacobian conjecture (Keller 1939); degree 2: Wang 1980; 2026 counterexamples: arXiv:2608.00222, arXiv:2609.17795, arXiv:2607.22198, arXiv:2607.18186 (Alpöge, van den Essen et al.)
premise_risks: arXiv:2608.00222, arXiv:2609.17795, arXiv:2607.22198, arXiv:2607.18186 (2026 preprints, unrefereed; one has an Isabelle AFP formalization): existence of non-injective Keller maps of C^3 of degree 7, i.e. the upper bound d_3 <= 7 and the claim that the Jacobian conjecture fails in dimension 3. Claim (cubic case) does not logically depend on them.
plain: The 2026 counterexamples to the Jacobian conjecture in three variables have degree 7 at best (Alpöge's map has component degrees 7,6,4). Wang's theorem says degree 2 is impossible. Find the smallest degree a three-variable counterexample can have: some number from 3 to 7.
math: Call F ∈ C[x,y,z]^3 a Keller map if det JF ∈ C^×, and let deg F = max_i deg F_i. Prove or disprove: every Keller map F : C^3 → C^3 with deg F <= 3 is injective (equivalently, by Białynicki-Birula-Rosenlicht and the Keller condition, a polynomial automorphism); i.e. d_3 >= 4. (Known: 3 <= d_3 <= 7, where d_3 is the least degree of a non-injective Keller map of C^3.)

title: Smallest degree of a Keller counterexample in dimension 3
premise_risks: Alpöge counterexample (2026 preprints in refs, e.g. arXiv:2608.00222; formally checked in Isabelle AFP 'Jacobian_Counterexample'): gives d_3 <= 7, i.e. that d_3 is finite. The Claim (d_3 <= 5) does not depend on it.
Other 2026 preprints (2609.17795, 2607.20210, 2607.22198, 2610.24889, 2607.21572, 2609.33491): further counterexamples of degree >= 7 in dim 3 and low-degree ones in dims 4-12; background.
plain: In 2026 the Jacobian conjecture was refuted in three variables. The first explicit counterexample (Alpöge's map) has polynomial degree 7. Wang's theorem says degree 2 is impossible. What is the smallest degree a counterexample in three variables can have? In particular, is there one of degree 3, 4 or 5?
math: Let $d_3$ be the least $d$ such that some polynomial map $F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with $\max_i\deg F_i=d$ and $\det DF\in\mathbb C^\times$ is not an automorphism. Wang's theorem gives $d_3\ge3$, and Alpöge's map gives $d_3\le7$. Determine $d_3$. In particular, decide whether $d_3\le5$.

title: Smallest dimension of a cubic-homogeneous Jacobian counterexample
credit: Classical HJC(n,3) program: Bass–Connell–Wright (1982), Yagzhev; Hubbers (n ≤ 4 classification); de Bondt–van den Essen arXiv:1609.09753; upper bound de Bondt arXiv:2610.24889.
premise_risks: arXiv:2610.24889 (de Bondt, Oct 2026, unrefereed, partly AI-written): source of N₃ ≤ 18 via HJC(18,3); only the upper bound depends on it.
arXiv:2608.00222 / arXiv:2609.17795 (2026 preprints, Alpöge's map and follow-up): the premise that the Jacobian conjecture is false at all; the formal Claim (dimension 5) does not depend on it.
plain: The Jacobian conjecture is now known to fail. A classical reduction says that if it fails at all, it fails for maps of the special form x + (cubic homogeneous terms), but the reduction pays for this by raising the number of variables. Such a cubic counterexample is now known in 18 variables, and none exists in 4 or fewer. What is the smallest number of variables in which one exists?
math: Let $N_3$ be the least $n$ such that there is $H=(H_1,\dots,H_n)$, each $H_i\in\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ homogeneous of degree 3, with $JH$ nilpotent (equivalently, for homogeneous $H$, $\det(I+JH)=1$) and $x+H$ not an automorphism of $\mathbb C^n$. Hubbers' classification of cubic homogeneous nilpotent Jacobians for $n\le4$ gives $N_3\ge5$ ($n=5$ is open as far as we know). De Bondt (arXiv:2610.24889, unrefereed), building on Alp\"oge's map and improving Van Rijn's 19, gives $N_3\le18$. Determine $N_3$; in particular, decide whether the Jacobian conjecture holds for cubic homogeneous maps in dimension 5. Companion: let $d_3$ be the least $\max_i\deg F_i$ over non-invertible Keller maps $F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ ($\det JF\in\mathbb C^*$). Wang's theorem gives $d_3\ge3$ and Alp\"oge's map gives $d_3\le7$.

title: Which monodromy groups do Jacobian counterexamples have?
premise_risks: The premise that the Jacobian conjecture was refuted in 2026 rests on 2026 preprints (arXiv:2607.20210, 2607.21572, 2608.00222); if those counterexamples fail, the set M is empty and the question changes completely.
arXiv:2608.02863 (Kistner-Shaska, 2026 preprint): source of S_d, A_d (d = 6, 12, families) as realized monodromy groups.
arXiv:2609.33491 (Fonollosa, 2026 preprint): source of imprimitive wreath-type monodromy groups.
plain: A Keller map (polynomial map with constant nonzero Jacobian) that is not invertible covers a generic point d times, and following the d preimages around loops gives a permutation group, its monodromy. Campbell's 1973 theorem says that if this group is regular (the Galois case), the map is invertible. The 2026 counterexamples realize full symmetric groups and some imprimitive groups. Is Campbell's theorem the only obstruction?
math: For a Keller map $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$ ($\det JF\in\mathbb C^\times$) of geometric degree $d\ge2$, let $\mathrm{Mon}(F)\le S_d$ be the geometric monodromy group (Galois group of the Galois closure of $\mathbb C(x)/\mathbb C(F)$ acting on the $d$ embeddings). It is transitive, and by Campbell's theorem it is regular only if $d=1$. Let $\mathcal M$ be the set of transitive groups (up to permutation isomorphism) arising as $\mathrm{Mon}(F)$ for non-invertible Keller maps in some dimension; $\mathcal M$ contains $S_d$, $A_d$ (e.g. $d=6,12$ and the families of Kistner-Shaska 2608.02863) and imprimitive wreath-type groups (Fonollosa 2609.33491), and is closed under direct products in product action ($F\times G$). Is $\mathcal M$ exactly the set of non-regular transitive groups? Test case: does some primitive group not containing $A_d$ (e.g. $\mathrm{AGL}(1,p)$ for a prime $p\ge5$, or $\mathrm{PSL}(2,7)$ on 7 points) lie in $\mathcal M$? (A negative answer to the test case means every primitive member of $\mathcal M$ is alternating or symmetric, which would refute the first question.)

title: Hearing tetrahedra
credit: Extends Durso (1988, MIT thesis) and Grieser-Maronna, 'Hearing the shape of a triangle' (Notices AMS 2013, arXiv:1208.3163); Kac's question.
results: The heat-invariant count is correct. The polyhedral Dirichlet heat trace gives volume, surface area, the edge sum of L_e times a function of the dihedral angle, and a vertex term (not explicit for general solid angles): 4 numbers against 6 congruence parameters. So the heat trace alone is insufficient.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.28602 (Krejcirik, 2026 survey): used only for the openness check (does not settle the problem); the statement itself assumes nothing from it.
plain: Triangles can be heard: their Dirichlet spectrum determines them up to congruence (Durso 1988; Grieser–Maronna 2013). Show the same for tetrahedra.
math: Let $T_1,T_2\subset\mathbb R^3$ be (nondegenerate) tetrahedra whose Dirichlet Laplacian eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, coincide. Prove that $T_1$ and $T_2$ are congruent.

title: Jacobi matrix of primes
plain: Build an infinite tridiagonal (Jacobi) matrix with zero diagonal and the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, ... on the off-diagonals. The standard criteria for purely absolutely continuous spectrum need the off-diagonal sequence to vary regularly, and they just fail because prime gaps fluctuate. Decide whether the spectrum is nevertheless purely absolutely continuous on the whole real line.
math: Let $J$ be the self-adjoint Jacobi operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ given by $(Ju)_n=p_{n-1}u_{n-1}+p_nu_{n+1}$ (with $p_0u_0:=0$), where $p_n$ is the $n$-th prime. It is self-adjoint by Carleman's criterion, since $\sum1/p_n=\infty$. Decide whether $\sigma(J)=\sigma_{ac}(J)=\mathbb R$ with no singular part.

title: Additive excess for sorting pattern-avoiding sequences
credit: Fredman 1976 (sorting with partial information); Opler, arXiv:2409.07868 (ESA 2025), sorting pattern-avoiding permutations
results: delta_tau >= 0: information-theoretic bound C_tau(n) >= log2|Av_n(tau)| (trivial). delta_tau <= 2: Fredman (1976), any set G of permutations can be sorted with log2|G| + 2n comparisons. Opler (arXiv 2409.07868) gives O((log c_tau +1)n), optimal only up to a constant factor. delta_tau = 0 is known for tau of length 3 in the 132-class (stack sorting, <=2n vs log2 C_n = 2n - O(log n)).
plain: Sorting an array promised to avoid a fixed pattern needs at least log2 of the number of allowed orders comparisons, and Fredman's theorem says 2n more always suffice. How many extra comparisons per element are really needed? Show that fewer than 2n extra suffice for 1324-avoiding inputs, or show that a linear excess is necessary for some pattern.
math: For a permutation τ let C_τ(n) be the minimum worst-case number of comparisons of a decision tree (knowing τ) that sorts a_1,…,a_n under the promise that their order pattern lies in Av_n(τ), and δ_τ = limsup_n (C_τ(n) − log_2|Av_n(τ)|)/n ∈ [0,2]. Prove or disprove: δ_τ = 0 for every permutation τ.

title: Codes avoiding square distances
results: Small values A(1..7)=1,2,4,5,10,12,14 re-verified by exact max-clique. Frankl-Rodl rate<1 argument is correct. The claim that codes with all distances between consecutive squares are polynomial is only correct for windows at linear distance. Constant-weight codes with w~k^2/2, w~n^{2/3}, and pairwise intersections <k have all distances in (k^2,(k+1)^2).
plain: Find the largest set of binary strings of length n in which no two differ in a perfect-square number of positions. Does it grow exponentially in n, and if so at what rate? This is a hypercube version of Sarkozy's theorem on square differences.
math: Let $A(n)=\max\{|C|: C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ d_H(x,y)\notin\{1,4,9,16,\dots\}\ \forall x\ne y\in C\}$. Decide whether $A(n)=2^{o(n)}$. More precisely, determine $\liminf_n\frac1n\log_2A(n)$ and $\limsup_n\frac1n\log_2A(n)$ (in particular whether they are equal).

title: Monochromatic square-sum triangles, many colours
credit: Khalfalah–Szemerédi (2006), monochromatic x+y = z² for finite colourings.
plain: Colour the positive integers with finitely many colours. Show there are always three different numbers of the same colour whose three pairwise sums are all perfect squares.
math: Prove that for every $r\ge1$ and every colouring $\chi:\mathbb N\to\{1,\dots,r\}$ there exist distinct $a,b,c\in\mathbb N$ with $\chi(a)=\chi(b)=\chi(c)$ and $a+b,\ a+c,\ b+c$ all perfect squares. (Equivalently: the triangle hypergraph of the graph on $\mathbb N$ with $a\sim b\iff a+b=\square$ has infinite chromatic number.)

title: Paley spin glass
results: Correct. Q is circulant with eigenvalues chi(a)sqrt p (Gauss sums), so E_p<=p^{3/2}/2. Square-wave ratio is (4/pi^2)sum_{m odd}chi(m)/m^2 + o(1); taking p=1 mod 8 and p=1 mod q for odd q<=y (reciprocity + Dirichlet) gives limsup=1/2. Recomputed p=53881: 0.4925. Bonus: the sum is >=2-pi^2/8 so liminf>=0.31.
plain: Place a ±1 spin at each element of F_p, and let each pair interact through the Legendre symbol of their difference. Equivalently, this is the max-cut problem for the Paley graph. The eigenvalue bound caps the ground-state energy at p^{3/2}/2. Simple square-wave configurations reach this bound along special primes, but heuristic search for typical primes stalls around 0.46. Is the eigenvalue bound asymptotically sharp for all primes?
math: For primes $p\equiv1\pmod4$ let $E_p=\max_{\sigma\in\{\pm1\}^{\mathbb F_p}}\sum_{i<j}\left(\frac{j-i}{p}\right)\sigma_i\sigma_j$. The circulant matrix $Q=\big(\big(\frac{j-i}p\big)\big)_{i,j\in\mathbb F_p}$ is symmetric with eigenvalues $\pm\sqrt p$ (each with multiplicity $\frac{p-1}2$) and $0$, so $E_p\le\frac12p^{3/2}$. (For the Paley graph $P_p$, $\mathrm{surp}(P_p)=\mathrm{maxcut}(P_p)-\frac12|E(P_p)|\le \frac14E_p+\frac p8$.) It is known that $\limsup_p E_p/p^{3/2}=\frac12$: if $(\frac qp)=1$ for all primes $q\le y$, then $\sigma_x=\operatorname{sgn}\cos(2\pi x/p)$ has ratio $\frac12-o_y(1)$; and the same $\sigma$ gives $E_p/p^{3/2}\ge\frac4{\pi^2}\big(2-\frac{\pi^2}8\big)-o(1)\approx0.31$ for every $p$. Determine $\liminf_{p}E_p/p^{3/2}$; in particular, is it $\frac12$?

title: Periodic optimal colourings of Cayley graphs of Z^2
credit: Posed for lattice Cayley graphs in 'The chromatic number of 4-dimensional lattices', arXiv:2407.03513 (2024); related: periodic colourings of quasi-transitive graphs, arXiv:2411.01951 (2024).
results: No proof is claimed. The decidability corollary is correct: compactness (de Bruijn-Erdos) semi-decides chi>k, and enumerating periodic colourings (torus quotients) semi-decides chi<=k if the answer is yes. A Z^2 SFT with one period also has a fully periodic point, so 'periodic point' is unambiguous here.
premise_risks: arXiv:2607.26942 (2026 preprint) is in refs; the statement does not depend on it.
plain: Join two points of the integer grid when their difference lies in a fixed finite set D. If this graph can be properly coloured with k colours, can it always be coloured with k colours in a repeating, wallpaper-like pattern? On a line the answer is yes. For some infinite graphs built from trees it is no. The plane is the first open case, and a yes would also give an algorithm for the chromatic number.
math: For finite symmetric $D\subset\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}$ let $G_D=\mathrm{Cay}(\mathbb Z^2,D)$ with $\chi(G_D)=k<\infty$. Must $G_D$ have a proper $k$-colouring invariant under a finite-index subgroup of $\mathbb Z^2$? Equivalently, does the $k$-colouring subshift $X_{D,k}\subset\{1..k\}^{\mathbb Z^2}$ always contain a periodic point? (A yes makes $\{(D,k):\chi(G_D)\le k\}$ decidable via compactness plus enumeration of periodic colourings. A no gives the first weakly aperiodic colouring subshift on $\mathbb Z^2$.) Same question for $\mathbb Z^d$, $d\ge3$.

title: A uniformly samplable counterexample to the poly-time low-degree conjecture
credit: Mao, The Polynomial-Time Low-Degree Conjecture is False, arXiv:2607.20318 (2026), Sec. 4.
premise_risks: arXiv:2607.20318 (Mao, 2026 preprint): the whole problem assumes Mao's construction (Reed-Muller subspace/trace functions, the advice size, the linear-time rank test after resampling) is correct.
arXiv:2505.17360 (Buhai-Hsieh-Jain-Kothari, 2025 preprint): background quasi-polynomial counterexample; status of refereeing not verified.
plain: Mao's counterexample (permutation-invariant graph distributions with zero low-degree advantage up to degree Theta(log^{r-1} n) that a linear-time rank test detects after constant-rate resampling) needs non-uniform advice for its Reed-Muller subspace / evaluation-point seed. Find a polynomial-time algorithm that outputs a good seed, giving a uniformly poly-time samplable counterexample; or show that every uniformly samplable permutation-invariant distribution with vanishing degree-polylog advantage is hard for poly-time noise-robust tests (a repaired conjecture).
math: For some fixed r >= 3, give a single randomized algorithm that, given 1^n, samples in expected poly(n) time from a permutation-invariant distribution P_n on n-vertex graphs whose low-degree advantage over G(n,1/2) tends to 0 at degree D_n = ceil(c0 (log n)^{r-1}) (some c0 > 0), while after independent edge resampling at a fixed rate delta in (0,1) a deterministic poly-time test distinguishes it from G(n,1/2) with both error probabilities -> 0. (Sufficient route via Mao's construction: find in poly(n) time evaluation points with every <= L of the vectors phi(x_i) linearly independent.)
refs: Mao, The Polynomial-Time Low-Degree Conjecture is False, arXiv:2607.20318
Buhai, Hsieh, Jain, Kothari, The Quasi-Polynomial Low-Degree Conjecture is False, arXiv:2505.17360
Hopkins, Statistical inference and the sum of squares method, PhD thesis 2018

title: All-Edges Sparse Triangle below m^{4/3} on balanced instances
credit: Alman, Vassilevska Williams 2026, arXiv:2610.06783, Sec. 6; Patrascu, STOC 2010
premise_risks: arXiv:2610.06783 (Alman-Vassilevska Williams, Oct 2026, unrefereed): the claim that lopsided AE-Sparse-Triangle (and 3SUM, APSP) are now truly subquadratic/subcubic, and that balanced instances remain open, i.e. the reason this is the live question and that 3SUM-based m^{4/3} hardness has fallen.
plain: Solve All-Edges Sparse Triangle (for each of m edges, report whether it is in a triangle) in O(m^{4/3-eps}) time on general (balanced) sparse graphs, or derive an m^{4/3-o(1)} lower bound from a hypothesis that survives AVW (e.g. 4SUM, OV/SETH, or combinatorial BMM).
math: Model: word-RAM with Θ(log N)-bit words. Is there a fixed ε > 0 such that for all constants α, δ > 0 there is a randomized (success ≥ 2/3) algorithm that, given a tripartite graph on parts A, B, C with |A|=|B|=|C|=N, m ≥ α N^{3/2} edges and maximum degree ≤ δ√N, decides for every edge whether it lies in a triangle in time O(m^{4/3-ε})? (The conditional-hardness alternative is a separate question.)
review_note: Context (Nov 2026): the OpenAI preprint refuting ETH/SETH removes the OV-based hardness route; the algorithmic question here is unaffected.
refs: Alman, Vassilevska Williams, Truly Subquadratic 3SUM and Truly Subcubic APSP via Triangles in Sparse Lopsided Graphs, arXiv:2610.06783 (Oct 2026)
Patrascu, Towards polynomial lower bounds for dynamic problems, STOC 2010
Kopelowitz, Pettie, Porat, Higher lower bounds from the 3SUM conjecture, SODA 2016

title: All-Edges Triangle in the (n, n, sqrt n) tripartite regime
credit: Alman, Vassilevska Williams, 'Truly Subquadratic 3SUM and Truly Subcubic APSP via Triangles in Sparse Lopsided Graphs', arXiv:2610.06783 (2026)
premise_risks: arXiv:2610.06783 (Alman-Vassilevska Williams, Oct 2026, unrefereed): source of the regime, of the refutation of the APSP-type hardness at this boundary, and of the m^{4/3} balanced-hardness framing.
arXiv:2610.17420 (Majdoddin, Oct 2026, unrefereed): extension of thin products to middle part D <= N^{0.172}, cited as the best partial progress.
plain: Given a tripartite graph with parts of sizes n, n, sqrt(n) and O(n^{3/2}) edges, determine for every edge whether it lies in a triangle in O(n^{2-eps}) time (combinatorial or algebraic).
math: Is there ε > 0 and a randomized word-RAM algorithm that, for every tripartite graph on A, B, C with |A| = |B| = n, |C| = ceil(sqrt n) and O(n^{3/2}) edges, decides for every edge whether it lies in a triangle in time O(n^{2-ε})? (Main question; a fine-grained reduction from balanced All-Edges Sparse Triangle at m^{4/3-o(1)} would be evidence for a negative answer but is not itself a disproof.)
refs: Alman, Vassilevska Williams, Truly Subquadratic 3SUM and Truly Subcubic APSP via Triangles in Sparse Lopsided Graphs, arXiv:2610.06783 (Oct 2026)

title: Beyond the D <= N^{0.172} wall for thin matrix products
credit: Majdoddin, Thin matrix products up to D ≤ N^0.172 and lossless reductions for 3SUM, Exact Triangle and APSP, arXiv:2610.17420 (Oct 2026); building on Alman–Vassilevska Williams arXiv:2610.06783.
premise_risks: arXiv:2610.06783 (Alman–Vassilevska Williams, Oct 2026 preprint): assumes the thin-product subroutine and the subquadratic 3SUM / subcubic APSP refutation.
arXiv:2610.17420 (Majdoddin, Oct 2026 preprint): assumes ε* ≥ ln4/(5 ln5) and that ⟨34,2,35⟩ is open.
arXiv:2610.42012 (Chan–Itakura–Ma–Yu, Nov 2026 preprint): makes the stated 3SUM payoff stale (3SUM already O(n^1.965)).
github.com/shreshth-s/thin-matrix-results (unrefereed repository) in refs.
plain: AVW's core subroutine computes requested entries of XY (N x D times D x N, D <= N^{eps}) in N^2/D^{c} operations; Majdoddin extends the regime to eps < ln4/(5 ln5) ~ 0.17227, matching Coppersmith's 1982 exponent for the same tensor. Either (a) extend the thin-product theorem to some eps > 0.17227 (e.g. via a different base identity, or settle Majdoddin's open thin product <34,2,35>), giving 3SUM/APSP exponents below 1.9945 / 2.9945; or (b) prove that every partial-product-tensor/Coppersmith-style scheme is limited to eps <= 0.17227.
math: Call ε good if there is γ > 0 such that for every constant K some deterministic word-RAM algorithm, given 1 ≤ D ≤ N^ε, X ∈ ℤ^{N×D}, Y ∈ ℤ^{D×N} with |entries| ≤ N^K and a list of at most N²/√D index pairs, outputs those entries of XY in O(N²/D^γ) time. Let ε* = sup of good ε. Is ε* > ln4/(5 ln5)? (Barrier version (b) is a separate question.)

Majdoddin, Thin matrix products up to D<=N^0.172 and lossless reductions for 3SUM, Exact Triangle and APSP, arXiv:2610.17420 (Oct 2026)

title: Finding Huang's vertex
results: The PPP-hardness reduction is correct. Take n=m+2. Pad 2^m real pigeons with 2^m+1 dummies, mapped injectively to the 2^m+1 dummy holes. Send the pigeon with C(x)=0 to dummy hole #1, so a collision with dummy #1 decodes to a zero-solution. Embed holes as h -> (h, parity h), which gives even weight. No two even-weight strings are adjacent, so every solution is a collision that decodes to a PIGEON solution.
plain: Huang's theorem says that any set of more than half the corners of the n-cube contains a corner with at least √n neighbours in the set. When the set is listed by a small circuit, how hard is it to find such a corner, or a flaw in the listing? The problem is easily shown to be at least as hard as the pigeonhole class PPP. Is it in PPP, so that it is PPP-complete, or does Huang's linear-algebra proof make it harder?
math: HUANG (black-box form): the input is the table of f : [2^{n-1}+1] → {0,1}^n, read bit by bit. Output either i ≠ j in [2^{n-1}+1] with f(i) = f(j), or i, j_1, …, j_m in [2^{n-1}+1] with m = ⌈√n⌉ such that f(j_1),…,f(j_m) are distinct and each is at Hamming distance 1 from f(i). Claim: HUANG ∈ PPP^dt, i.e. there is a constant c such that for every n, HUANG_n reduces to PIGEON_m with m ≤ (n+2)^c by a decision-tree reduction of depth ≤ (n+2)^c. Every PIGEON input bit is a depth-bounded decision tree on the HUANG input, and every PIGEON solution maps back to a HUANG solution by such a tree. (The white-box circuit version follows from a uniform such reduction. The white-box negative answer would imply FP ≠ PPP. Which class contains HUANG if Claim fails is a follow-up and not part of Claim.)

title: From S_2E to E^NP: near-maximum circuit lower bounds
credit: Korten (FOCS 2021); Chen, Hirahara, Ren (STOC 2024), arXiv:2309.12912; Li (STOC 2024), arXiv:2310.17762.
premise_risks: ECCC TR26-118 (Ren–Williams, Jul 2026, unrefereed): status claim that E^{prMA}/1 requires 2^n/n circuits; only affects the 'state of the art' summary, not the statement.
arXiv:2605.03306 (Hitchcock, May 2026 preprint): comeagerness result in S₂E; context only.
plain: Prove E^NP is not contained in SIZE[2^n/n] (or even SIZE[2^{epsilon n}] for some eps>0 infinitely often); equivalently, put Range Avoidance in FP^NP for the relevant circuit classes, improving Li's FS_2^P algorithm.
math: Prove that for some ε > 0 there is L ∈ E^NP such that for infinitely many n, L ∩ {0,1}^n has no circuit of size 2^{εn} (stronger: for all large n). Related target (not claimed equivalent at this size): AVOID ∈ FP^NP, which by Korten (2021) implies E^NP ⊄ SIZE[2^n/n].
review_note: Context (AI-lab announcement, treated as correct): OpenAI 378, The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False. Claims superlinear circuit lower bounds for a language in E^NP on infinitely many lengths, which is new for E^NP. Superlinear is far below the board's 2^{eps n} target, so this does not resolve it, but it changes the stated best-known E^NP lower bound.
refs: Chen, Hirahara, Ren, Symmetric exponential time requires near-maximum circuit size, STOC 2024, arXiv:2309.12912
Li, Symmetric exponential time requires near-maximum circuit size: simplified, truly uniform, STOC 2024, arXiv:2310.17762
Hitchcock, Exponential-size circuit complexity is comeager in symmetric exponential time, arXiv:2605.03306

title: Optimal dimension dependence in the smoothed complexity of the simplex method
credit: Bach, Huiberts, Optimal smoothed analysis of the simplex method, arXiv:2504.04197 (2025; v2 May 2026).
premise_risks: arXiv:2504.04197 (Bach-Huiberts; v2 May 2026, refereed status not verified): source of both the upper bound σ^{-1/2} d^{11/4} log^{7/4} n and the diameter lower bound.
plain: Bach and Huiberts (2025) found a simplex method with smoothed complexity O(σ^{-1/2} d^{11/4} log^{7/4} n) pivots and showed σ^{-1/2} is optimal. In the dimension d, the best lower bound is only about d^{1/2}. Close the gap in d.
math: Model: rows (ā_i, b̄_i) ∈ ℝ^{d+1}, i ≤ n, of Euclidean norm ≤ 1, each perturbed by independent N(0, σ² I), giving P = {x : ⟨a_i,x⟩ ≤ b_i}. Let diam(P) be the combinatorial diameter of its vertex-edge graph. Known (Bach–Huiberts): E[diam] = Ω(σ^{-1/2} d^{1/2} (ln 4/σ)^{-1/4}) at n = ⌊(4/σ)^d⌋, and a simplex method with O(σ^{-1/2} d^{11/4} log^{7/4} n) pivots exists. Claim: there are b > 1/2, c > 0 and K such that for all large d and all 0 < σ ≤ 1/d, some n ≤ (4/σ)^{Kd} and some unperturbed rows of norm ≤ 1 give E[diam(P)] ≥ c σ^{-1/2} d^b (log 4/σ)^{-K}. (The companion algorithmic question, whether a polynomial-time-per-pivot rule with Phase I achieves O(σ^{-1/2} d^a (log n)^{O(1)}) for some a < 11/4, has no canonical formal model and is not part of Claim.)

title: Proof complexity of the sensitivity theorem
plain: Huang proved that any set of more than half the corners of the n-cube contains a corner with at least √n neighbours inside the set. Write this as a propositional formula with one variable per corner. Do polynomial-size proofs exist in resolution, cutting planes or sum-of-squares, measured against the 2^n variables?
math: Let N = 2^n, K = 2^{n-1}+1, d = ⌈√n⌉ − 1. SENS_n is the CNF on main variables x_v (v ∈ {0,1}^n) and sequential-counter variables s_{i,j} (0 ≤ i ≤ N, 0 ≤ j ≤ K). It consists of (i) the counter clauses (s_{N,K}); (¬s_{0,j}) for 1 ≤ j ≤ K; (¬s_{i,j} ∨ s_{i−1,j} ∨ x_i) and (¬s_{i,j} ∨ s_{i−1,j} ∨ s_{i−1,j−1}) for 1 ≤ i ≤ N, 1 ≤ j ≤ K, with x_1,…,x_N the main variables in a fixed order; together these say ∑_v x_v ≥ K; and (ii) the clauses ¬x_v ∨ ⋁_{u∈U} ¬x_u for every v and every (d+1)-set U of neighbours of v. Its size is N^{O(1)}: Θ(N·K) counter clauses plus N^{1+o(1)} neighbourhood clauses. It is unsatisfiable by Huang's theorem. Does SENS_n have refutations of size N^{O(1)} in (a) resolution, (b) cutting planes (size counted in bits), or (c) sum-of-squares of degree O(log N)? Claim: at least one of (a), (b), (c) holds. Each part is also stated separately. Lower bounds 2^{N^{Ω(1)}} are equally of interest.

title: Three collinear points after the fall of 3SUM
credit: Alman & Vassilevska Williams, 'Truly Subquadratic 3SUM and Truly Subcubic APSP via Triangles in Sparse Lopsided Graphs', arXiv:2610.06783 (2026), Sec. 1 and Sec. 6.
premise_risks: AVW arXiv:2610.06783 (2026 preprint): truly subquadratic 3SUM, the premise that removes the 3SUM-based lower bound for collinearity.
Majdoddin arXiv:2610.17420 (2026 preprint): improved thin-matrix-product reductions for 3SUM/APSP; supporting background.
Chan–Itakura–Ma–Yu arXiv:2610.42012 (2026 preprint): derandomization of real 3SUM; supporting background.
Fischer arXiv:2610.32162 (2026 preprint): k-AP-based GeomBase lower bounds explicitly not covering collinearity; used to argue the question is still open.
plain: Given n points in the plane (integer coordinates poly(n), or real RAM), decide whether three are collinear in O(n^{2-eps}) time for some eps>0; or give a fine-grained reduction showing Collinearity is hard under a hypothesis not refuted by Alman-Vassilevska Williams (e.g. 4SUM, 3SUM-Indexing, or a new geometric hypothesis).
math: Prove or disprove: for every constant c ≥ 1 there are ε > 0 and a deterministic word-RAM algorithm (word size Θ(log n)) deciding in O(n^{2-ε}) time whether n distinct points of ℤ² ∩ [−n^c, n^c]² contain three collinear points. (The real-RAM variant is a separate question.)
refs: Alman, Vassilevska Williams, Truly Subquadratic 3SUM and Truly Subcubic APSP via Triangles in Sparse Lopsided Graphs, arXiv:2610.06783 (Oct 2026)
Majdoddin, Thin matrix products up to D<=N^0.172 and lossless reductions for 3SUM, Exact Triangle and APSP, arXiv:2610.17420 (Oct 2026)
Gajentaan, Overmars, On a class of O(n^2) problems in computational geometry, CGTA 1995

title: Chaos in the double pendulum at every energy
plain: The planar double pendulum with equal masses and equal arms looks chaotic at moderate energies but almost regular at very low and very high energies. Prove that it has genuine (positive-entropy) chaos at every energy above the rest state.
math: Let $H(\theta_1,\theta_2,p_1,p_2)$ be the Hamiltonian of the planar double pendulum with $m_1=m_2=\ell_1=\ell_2=g=1$ on $T^*\mathbb T^2$, with minimum value $E_0$ (the hanging rest state). Prove that for every $E>E_0$ the Hamiltonian flow restricted to $\{H=E\}$ has positive topological entropy.

title: Chaos in the symmetric ABC flow
credit: T. Dombre, U. Frisch, J. M. Greene, M. Henon, A. Mehr, A. M. Soward, 'Chaotic streamlines in the ABC flows', J. Fluid Mech. 167 (1986); V. I. Arnold (1965); M. Henon (1966).
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.17449 (Szuminski-Llibre, 2026 preprint): relied on only for the openness check (it is perturbative near the axes and does not settle A=B=C=1); the statement assumes nothing from it.
plain: The ABC flow with all three coefficients equal to 1 is the classical steady Euler flow on the 3-torus that is believed to be chaotic. Prove that it really is: show it has positive topological entropy.
math: Prove that the flow of $\dot x=\sin z+\cos y,\ \dot y=\sin x+\cos z,\ \dot z=\sin y+\cos x$ on $\mathbb{T}^3=(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})^3$ has positive topological entropy (e.g. by exhibiting a transversal homoclinic orbit to a hyperbolic periodic orbit, or a horseshoe for a Poincare map).

title: Deciding rationality of PL rotation numbers
credit: Belk, Hyde, Moore (2022), arXiv:2211.05825, Questions 3–4.
plain: A circle homeomorphism made of finitely many straight pieces, with rational break points and slopes, has a rotation number. Rational rotation numbers can be confirmed by finding a rational periodic orbit. Irrational ones occur too: Belk–Hyde–Moore found √2−1 with slopes 3/2, 2/3, 1. Is there an algorithm that always decides which case holds?
math: Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of orientation-preserving PL homeomorphisms of $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with finitely many rational break points, rational slopes and $f(0)\in\mathbb Q$, encoded by these data. Is $\{f\in\mathcal P:\rho(f)\in\mathbb Q\}$ decidable? (It is computably enumerable: if $\rho(f)=p/q$, the zero set of the lift $F^q(x)-x-p$ is a nonempty finite union of rational points and rational intervals.)

title: Ergodicity of the regular tetrahedron billiard
plain: A billiard ball bounces inside a regular tetrahedron. The tetrahedron does not tile space, and its dihedral angle arccos(1/3) is an irrational multiple of pi. So the billiard cannot be unfolded into a straight-line flow on a torus or a translation structure. Is the motion ergodic, so that almost every trajectory equidistributes in position and direction?
math: Let $\Delta\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a regular tetrahedron and $\phi_t$ the billiard flow on the unit tangent bundle $T^1\Delta$, with specular reflection at faces and orbits hitting edges or vertices discarded (a null set). Prove or disprove that $\phi_t$ is ergodic with respect to Liouville measure.

title: Is the Mandelbrot set decidable at Gaussian rationals?
credit: P. Potgieter, arXiv:cs/0604003 (2006), Sec. 2.3.
results: The reduction is correct apart from one flaw. A non-repelling cycle implies c in M, since by Fatou all cycles are repelling when c is outside M. The example arithmetic checks out: mu/2-mu^2/4=(37+16i)/100. But (*) as stated is FALSE. c=-2 and c=+-i are Gaussian-integer Misiurewicz parameters in M with all cycles repelling (c=i: 0->i->-1+i->-i->-1+i). The fix excludes Z[i], where membership is a finite check.
plain: Is there an algorithm that takes a complex number with rational real and imaginary parts and decides whether it lies in the Mandelbrot set? Escaping points can be confirmed, and so can points that have an attracting or neutral cycle of some period, since for each period that is an exact algebraic check. The trouble is points on the boundary where every cycle repels. No such Gaussian rational is known, but none has been ruled out.
math: Let $M=\{c\in\mathbb C:(f_c^{n}(0))_{n\ge0}\text{ bounded}\}$, $f_c(z)=z^2+c$. Prove or disprove that $M\cap\mathbb Q(i)$ is a decidable subset of $\mathbb Q(i)$. $\mathbb Q(i)\setminus M$ is r.e. For each $n$, the existence of an $n$-cycle with multiplier of modulus $\le1$ is decidable for algebraic $c$ (Tarski), and such a cycle forces $c\in M$. $M\cap\mathbb Z[i]$ is a finite, explicitly computable set (it contains the Misiurewicz points $-2,\pm i$, whose cycles are all repelling). So a positive answer would follow from (*): every $c\in(M\cap\mathbb Q(i))\setminus\mathbb Z[i]$ has a non-repelling cycle. Prove or disprove (*). (Example: $c=(37+16i)/100$ lies on the main cardioid with multiplier $(3+4i)/5$, a Siegel parameter.)

title: Is the measure of the hyperbolic real quadratic parameters computable?
results: Checked: λ(H) is lower semicomputable. Each CE(C,γ) piece is an intersection of finite-time conditions, so it is only upper semicomputable, which is the wrong direction. The 'equivalently' clause is valid through Lyubich's regular-or-stochastic theorem and Avila–Moreira (almost every stochastic parameter is CE).
premise_risks: arXiv 2505.20495 (Golmakani–Koudjinan–Luzzatto–Pilarczyk, 2025 preprint): cited only for the remark that computer-assisted schemes certify expansion, not measure; statement does not depend on it.
plain: For real c between −2 and 1/4, the map x ↦ x²+c has an attracting cycle for an open dense set of c, yet the chaotic parameters have positive length (Jakobson). Is the total length of the parameters with an attracting cycle a computable number? It can be approximated from below by listing windows, but no known method approximates it from above.
math: Let $H=\{c\in[-2,1/4]:\ x\mapsto x^2+c\text{ has an attracting periodic orbit}\}$. Is the Lebesgue measure $\lambda(H)$ a computable real number? ($H$ is open and its components can be certified by interval arithmetic, so $\lambda(H)$ is lower semicomputable; Jakobson's theorem gives $\lambda(H)<9/4$.) Equivalently: is the measure of the set of stochastic (Collet–Eckmann) parameters lower semicomputable?

title: Outer billiards around analytic tables with flat points
credit: Moser's boundedness question (J. Moser, Stable and Random Motions, 1973); Douady (thesis, 1982); Sorrentino arXiv:2610.06418 (2026) for the C^1-generic case.
results: I checked the singularity claim. At a flat point of order k the radius of curvature satisfies rho(theta)~|theta|^{-k/(k+1)} (|theta|^{-2/3} for x^4+y^4), and the tangency point q(p) is only C^{1/(k+1)} across the tangent lines at the flat points. So T and the limiting map at infinity are genuinely non-smooth, and KAM does not apply directly. The claim is correct.
premise_risks: arXiv:2610.06418 (Sorrentino, 2026 preprint): cited for C^1-generic unbounded orbits (centrally symmetric tables only); motivation only, the statement does not depend on it.
plain: Outer billiards around a smooth convex shape with positive curvature has only bounded orbits (Moser-Douady). Polygons, semicircles and generic C^1 shapes can have orbits that escape to infinity. What if the table is analytic and strictly convex, but its curvature vanishes at a few points, like the superellipse x^4+y^4 ≤ 1? Decide whether every orbit stays bounded.
math: Let $K\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a strictly convex body whose boundary is a real-analytic closed curve with curvature vanishing at at least one point (hence, by analyticity, at finitely many). For $p\in\mathbb R^2\setminus K$, let $T(p)=2q-p$, where $q\in\partial K$ is the tangency point of the tangent line from $p$ that has $K$ on its left. Is every $T$-orbit bounded, for every such $K$? If not, characterize the $K$ with unbounded orbits, e.g. by the vanishing orders of the curvature or by symmetry. First test case: $K=\{x^4+y^4\le1\}$.

title: Positive metric entropy of the Chirikov standard map at an explicit moderate parameter
credit: Ya. G. Sinai (conjecture, 1994); Slijepcevic 2026, arXiv:2611.09361
premise_risks: arXiv:2611.09361 (Slijepcevic, Nov 2026 preprint): the known result h_m(f_k) >= log(2 pi k+4) - 2^430 for k >= exp(2^50000), quoted as background only.
OpenAI preprint (unrefereed, credited in 2611.09361): non-effective positivity for large k, background only.
plain: Sinai conjectured that the standard map has positive metric entropy for every parameter k>0. After a 2026 AI-generated non-effective proof for large k, Slijepčević proved it for every k ≥ exp(2^{50000}). Bring the threshold down to a physically meaningful range, e.g. all k ≥ 10^6, or even a single explicit k ≤ 100.
math: Let f_k(x,y)=(x+y+k sin(2 pi x), y+k sin(2 pi x)) on T^2=R^2/Z^2 (Slijepcevic's normalization; Chirikov's K equals 2 pi k), and h_m(f_k) the metric entropy w.r.t. area. Known: log(2 pi k+4)-2^{430} <= h_m(f_k) <= log(2 pi k+4) for k>=exp(2^{50000}) (Slijepcevic 2026). Prove h_m(f_k)>0 for all k>=10^6, or for at least one explicit k<=100.
review_note: Context (AI-lab announcement, treated as correct): OpenAI 146: Positive metric entropy for the standard map (Positive Metric Entropy for the Standard Map at Large Parameters). Proves h_m(f_k)>0 for all k>=k_0 in the same normalization, but k_0 is not explicit (ineffective). The board asks for all k>=10^6 or one explicit k<=100, so it is not met. The 'Known' line should cite this all-large-k result alongside Slijepcevic's explicit exp(2^50000) threshold.

title: A monotile that forces quasicrystalline symmetry
credit: Einstein problem: Socolar-Taylor (2011, arXiv:1009.1419); Smith-Myers-Kaplan-Goodman-Strauss (2023, arXiv:2303.10798); Gummelt decagon covering (1996); Steinhardt-Jeong quasi-unit-cell model
plain: Every aperiodic monotile known (Socolar-Taylor, the hat, the spectre, and the 3D examples) has tilings with only crystallographic rotational structure: 2-, 3-, 4- or 6-fold. Is there a single tile in the plane whose tilings are all forced to be quasicrystalline with fivefold symmetry, as Penrose tilings are? Or is non-crystallographic symmetry something only two or more tiles can enforce?
math: Call a compact set T ⊂ ℝ² homeomorphic to a closed disc a monotile if it tiles ℝ² by isometric copies, reflections allowed. Does there exist a monotile T such that (i) every tiling by copies of T uses only finitely many orientations of T (up to translation), and (ii) for every such tiling 𝒯 the translation hull Ω(𝒯), the closure of {𝒯 + v} in the standard local topology (agreement on B(0,1/ε) after a translation of size < ε), is invariant under rotation by 2π/5? (Equivalently, the rotated tiling R𝒯 lies in Ω(𝒯).) The R³ icosahedral analogue is a secondary target.

title: A strongly aperiodic monotile in four dimensions
credit: Kamenetsky 2026, arXiv:2610.00916, Problem 9.1 (context: Smith-Myers-Kaplan-Goodman-Strauss 2023, arXiv:2303.10798; Tsiokos 2026, arXiv:2609.19214)
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.19214 (Tsiokos, 2026, unrefereed): the claimed strongly aperiodic 3D monotile Chair44 that motivates the question; Claim does not depend on it.
arXiv:2609.24779 (Goodman-Strauss, 2026, unrefereed): independent proof for Chair44; context only.
arXiv:2610.00916 (Kamenetsky, 2026, unrefereed): reports a failed 4D search and poses the problem; context only.
plain: The hat (2023) is a single shape that tiles the plane only non-periodically, and in 2026 a 3D analogue was announced (Chair44, a decorated chair-shaped polycube). Find one connected 4D shape whose copies fill 4D space, where no tiling by it is left unchanged by any translation.
math: Find a compact set $T\subset\mathbb R^4$ homeomorphic to a closed 4-ball such that (i) $\mathbb R^4$ admits a tiling by isometric copies of $T$ (reflections allowed; copies cover $\mathbb R^4$ with pairwise disjoint interiors), and (ii) no such tiling is invariant under any nonzero translation. (Drop the weak variant (ii'), or flag it as possibly easy via prisms over a 3D monotile.)

title: Beat the (1-o(1)) log2 d exponent in quasi-polynomial polytope diameter bounds
credit: Kalai-Kleitman 1992; Todd 2014 (arXiv:1402.3579); Sukegawa; Liu-Ge-Ye 2026 (arXiv:2609.33434)
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.33434 (Liu-Ge-Ye, 2026, unrefereed): the current best bound (n-d)^{log2 G_d}, G_d ~ (4 ln 2) d/(ln d)^2, and the claim that the leading term is sharp for path-counting recursions; recorded as context, Claim does not depend on it.
plain: All known bounds on the diameter of a d-dimensional polyhedron with n facets have the form (n−d)^{log₂ d − O(log log d)}. The latest (Liu–Ge–Ye 2026) is (n−d)^{log₂ G_d} with G_d ~ (4 ln 2) d/(ln d)². Get an exponent at most (1−ε) log₂ d.
math: Let $\Delta_u(d,n)$ be the maximum graph diameter of a pointed $d$-polyhedron with $n$ facets. Known: $\Delta_u(d,n)\le (n-d)^{\log_2 G_d}$, $G_d=(4\ln2+o(1))d/(\ln d)^2$ (Liu–Ge–Ye 2026), after Kalai–Kleitman, Todd, Sukegawa. Prove $\Delta_u(d,n)\le (n-d)^{(1-\varepsilon)\log_2 d}$ for some fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and all large $d$.
review_note: Context (AI-lab announcement, treated as correct): OpenAI 380, Superpolynomial graph diameter of simple polytopes (polynomial Hirsch refuted). Gives bounded simple polytopes with n facets, d=n^{o(1)}, diameter n^{omega(1)}, and Thm 1.2 lower bound cE*min{E^a,d^b}. Unquantified superpolynomial growth does not reach (n-d)^{(1-eps)log2 d}, so the upper-bound target stays open. The board's 'Known' line should add the new superpolynomial lower bound.

title: Gromov width of the 4D l^4 ball
results: c_G(U) >= pi: U contains the Euclidean unit ball, since sum x_i^4 <= (sum x_i^2)^2. (Trivial.) c_G(U) <= c_Z(U) = c_EHZ(U) = c0 = 4Gamma(5/4)^2/Gamma(3/2) ~ 3.7081 (arXiv 2609.37794, Thm 2 with n=2, p=4, B=D=I). Gromov width is <= every normalized capacity. The volume bound sqrt(2 Vol U) ~ 4.65 is weaker.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.37794 (2026, unrefereed): Thm 2 giving c_Z(U) = c_EHZ(U) = 4Γ(5/4)^2/Γ(3/2); the Claim's target value c0 comes from it. If that value is wrong, Claim may be false for a trivial reason.
plain: The 4D superball x1^4+y1^4+x2^4+y2^4 <= 1 contains the round unit ball, so it holds a symplectic ball of capacity pi. Its cylindrical capacity is about 3.708, and no symplectic ball can be bigger than that. Narrow the gap: embed a bigger ball, or show that no ball of capacity close to 3.708 fits.
math: Let U = {x1^4+y1^4+x2^4+y2^4 <= 1} ⊂ (R^4, ω0) and c_G(U) = sup{πr^2 : B^4(r) embeds symplectically in U}. Known: π <= c_G(U) <= c0 := 4Γ(5/4)^2/Γ(3/2) ≈ 3.7081 (= c_Z(U) = c_EHZ(U)). Prove or disprove: c_G(U) = c0 (i.e. U satisfies the strong Viterbo equality between Gromov width and cylindrical capacity).

title: How nearly can tetrahedra close up: the exponent
credit: Steinhaus problem; Świerczkowski (1959) non-closure; Elgersma & Wagon (2016), arXiv:1610.00280.
results: g(n) >= c*3^{-n/2} for all n (new, short proof): g_n = s_{i1}...s_{in}, linear part = ±R_q, q = v_{i1}...v_{in}, v_i the pure quaternions ±i±j±k (norm 3); non-backtracking => q primitive in the Hurwitz order (unique factorisation; checked by computer to n=11). If T_n is near T_0 the linear part is near a symmetry ±R_u; q*conj(u) cannot be real (primitivity / 2*3^n not a square), so its vector part has length >=1/2 while |q u| <= sqrt2*3^{n/2}, giving rotation error >> 3^{-n/2}.
premise_risks: QED-internal derivation (unrefereed): the bounds 1/12 ≤ κ ≤ 1/2 (Hurwitz-order primitivity checked by computer only to n = 11). The formal Claim only uses the definitions, not these bounds.
plain: Glue regular tetrahedra face to face in a chain of length n; it can never close exactly. How close to closing can it get? Short arguments show the best gap is at least about 3^{-n/2} and, for infinitely many n, at most about 3^{-n/12}; counting suggests 3^{-n/6}. Narrow the exponent range [1/12, 1/2].
math: Let g(k) be the minimal Hausdorff distance between T_k and T_0 over non-backtracking face-reflection chains of length k, and κ := liminf_{n→∞} −(1/n) log₃ min_{1≤k≤n} g(k). Known: 1/12 ≤ κ ≤ 1/2 (heuristic κ = 1/6). Prove κ > 1/12, i.e. there are δ > 0 and N such that for every n ≥ N some non-backtracking chain of length between 1 and n ends within 3^{−(1/12+δ)n} of T_0.

title: Superlinear unit distances on the unit sphere
credit: Erdős, Hickerson, Pach, 'A problem of Leo Moser about repeated distances on the sphere', Amer. Math. Monthly 96 (1989); Swanepoel-Valtr (2004)
plain: In 2026 a number-field construction showed that points in the plane can have n^(1+c) unit distances, disproving Erdos's conjecture. On a sphere of radius 1/sqrt2 an n^(4/3) construction is classical, but on the unit sphere only n·sqrt(log n) is known. Can the new ideas give a power gain there?
math: Prove or disprove: there is $c>0$ such that for infinitely many $n$ there exist $P\subset S^2=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^3:|x|=1\}$ with $|P|=n$ and $\#\{\{p,q\}\subset P:|p-q|=1\}\ge n^{1+c}$.

title: An explicit, checkable counterexample to Hadwiger's conjecture
premise_risks: OpenAI October 2026 release (Family 157), surveyed in arXiv:2610.17090 (unrefereed): the claim that Hadwiger's conjecture is false at all. If that disproof is wrong, the problem asks for something that may not exist, and its whole motivation collapses.
arXiv:2609.35361 and arXiv:2606.01586 (2026 preprints): background on the α ≤ 2 / connected-matching route and the size of known counterexamples.
plain: Hadwiger's conjecture says a graph that needs t colours contains the complete graph K_t as a minor. A disproof claimed in October 2026 (not yet peer reviewed) is non-constructive: it uses graphs with no three pairwise non-adjacent vertices, on roughly 2^(10^12) vertices or more, and never names a graph. Find one concrete graph on fewer than a million vertices for which the conjecture fails, with a proof that can be checked.
math: For a finite graph $G$ let $h(G)=\max\{t: K_t\preceq G\}$ be its Hadwiger number and $\chi(G)$ its chromatic number. Exhibit an explicit graph $G$ with $|V(G)|<10^6$ and $h(G)<\chi(G)$, with a complete proof of both bounds that can be checked (by hand or by a computer computation of feasible size). Sufficient route (Cambie): an explicit $G$ with $\alpha(G)\le2$, $|V(G)|=4t-1$ and no connected matching of size $t$ (a matching whose edges are pairwise joined by an edge of $G$) violates Hadwiger's conjecture.
review_note: Context: the OpenAI Hadwiger counterexample (preprint dated 2026-09-23, released 2026-10-06) is non-explicit (random graphs on 2^{1000·(10^9+1)·N} vertices); this problem asks for an explicit one. Context (AI-lab announcement, treated as correct): OpenAI 157: Graph coloring, clique minors, and Colin de Verdiere invariants (A counterexample to Hadwiger's conjecture). Hadwiger is now disproved (alpha<=2 graphs with cm(G)<m/100, h<26m/75+2/3<m/2<=chi). But the construction is probabilistic (sampled configurations, unbounded parameter n), so it gives no explicit graph with <10^6 vertices and a checkable proof. The board target is unmet; premise (a counterexample exists) is confirmed. Reframe as 'explicit/small' only.

title: Ringel for forests
credit: Ringel (1963); Montgomery-Pokrovskiy-Sudakov (arXiv:2001.02665); Keevash-Staden (arXiv:2004.09947); Barrientos-Minion, EJGTA 4(2) 2016 (ρ-labelled forests)
plain: Ringel's conjecture, now a theorem for large n, says the complete graph on 2m+1 vertices splits into 2m+1 copies of any tree with m edges. Show the same holds for every forest with m edges. A stronger form asks that every such forest have a rho-labelling, which gives a cyclic decomposition.
math: Prove that for every m ≥ 1 and every forest F with m edges and no isolated vertices, E(K_{2m+1}) can be partitioned into 2m+1 subgraphs each isomorphic to F. Stronger form: every such F admits a ρ-labelling.

title: Computable connective constants
plain: Count the self-avoiding walks of length n on the Cayley graph of a finitely generated group. Their n-th roots decrease to the connective constant, so it can always be approximated from above. For groups with a solvable word problem, can it always be computed to any precision, i.e. also approximated from below?
math: Let $G$ be a finitely generated group with solvable word problem, $S=S^{-1}$ a finite generating set, $c_n$ the number of $n$-step self-avoiding walks from $e$ in $\mathrm{Cay}(G,S)$, and $\mu(G,S)=\lim_n c_n^{1/n}=\inf_n c_n^{1/n}$ (a right-computable real). Is $\mu(G,S)$ always a computable real? If not, construct $(G,S)$ with solvable word problem and $\mu(G,S)$ non-computable. If so, is the map (word-problem algorithm, $S$) $\mapsto\mu(G,S)$ uniformly computable?

title: Deciding limit cycles
credit: Extension of Graca-Zhong (arXiv:2101.07701) noncomputability of planar periodic orbits; related: Hilbert's 16th problem, Il'yashenko on algebraic unsolvability of the center-focus problem.
results: The claim that hyperbolic limit cycles are r.e. via interval certification is correct. The remark that fixed-degree versions 'can become trivially decidable' is wrong. Each fixed-degree set is still infinite. Bautin's finite generation only gives non-uniform decidability of the local center condition, not of whether cycles exist.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.22058 (2026 preprint): cited only for the claim that the planar (N=2) case is open and that Lyapunov stability is undecidable in dimension 5; the statement does not depend on it.
plain: Given a polynomial vector field in the plane with rational coefficients, is there an algorithm that decides whether it has a limit cycle, that is, an isolated closed orbit? Hilbert's 16th problem asks how many limit cycles there can be. This asks only whether their existence is algorithmically decidable. The same question can be asked for closed orbits of any kind, including those in period annuli around centres.
math: Let $\mathcal L=\{(P,Q)\in\mathbb Q[x,y]^2:\ \dot x=P,\dot y=Q$ has a limit cycle, i.e. a non-constant periodic orbit that has a neighbourhood containing no other periodic orbit$\}$ and $\mathcal P=\{(P,Q):$ the system has a non-constant periodic orbit in $\mathbb R^2\}$, with inputs given by their rational coefficient lists (degree unbounded). (a) Is $\mathcal L$ decidable? (b) Is $\mathcal P$ decidable? (c) Are $\mathcal L,\mathcal P$ or their complements recursively enumerable? (d) Same questions restricted to degree 2.
review_note: Context (Nov 2026): OpenAI claims uniform bounds for Hilbert's 16th problem; that does not decide existence of limit cycles, which this problem asks.

title: Spikes at the squares
credit: Cheon, Exner, Šeba (2000), arXiv:quant-ph/0004058 (continuum analogue with spikes at the squares).
results: Correct with a caveat. The spike gaps are 2m+1, so the spike-to-spike map is C·R(k(2m+1)), a one-frequency analytic cocycle over rotation by 2k. Herman's subharmonicity gives L ≥ log|C_11| = log sqrt(1+λ²/(4sin²k)). This bounds the phase-averaged exponent only: at the fixed phase θ=k (coupled to the frequency) the limit is not guaranteed, so eigenfunction decay is heuristic.
plain: On the half-line lattice, add a fixed spike of height λ at every perfect square. The free band (-2,2) then has no absolutely continuous spectrum, by Remling's theorem. Decide whether the spectrum inside the band is pure point (localized states) or singular continuous. A heuristic in the physics literature predicts singular continuous.
math: Let $(Hu)(n)=u(n+1)+u(n-1)+\lambda\,\mathbf 1_{\{m^2:m\ge1\}}(n)\,u(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, $u(0)=0$, $\lambda\ne0$ fixed, and let $\mu$ be the spectral measure of $\delta_1$. Determine the spectral type of $\mu|_{(-2,2)}$: is it pure point, purely singular continuous, or mixed? (Known: $\mu_{ac}=0$ by Remling's theorem. Cheon–Exner–Šeba heuristically predict purely singular continuous spectrum for the continuum analogue; positive Lyapunov exponents of the spike-to-spike cocycle suggest pure point.)

title: Ten Martini for the kagome lattice
credit: Extends Avila–Jitomirskaya (Ten Martini, Annals 2009) and Becker–Han–Jitomirskaya–Zworski (honeycomb, arXiv:1803.00988).
results: Found during review (Nov 2026): the general version fails. Replace each vertical edge of Z^2 by a rhombus (i,j)–(i±w,j+1/2)–(i,j+1) with w=1/(2√2) and take B=π/w: each rhombus carries flux π, α=√2 is irrational, and Aharonov–Bohm caging decouples the rows, giving σ(H_B)={0}∪±[√5−1,√5+1], which contains intervals. The problem is therefore restricted to the kagome lattice, a natural case where this caging cannot occur.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.15812 (2026 preprint): 1D Robust Ten Martini; cited as a possible tool only, M does not depend on it.
arXiv:2611.10767 (2026 preprint): cited; M does not depend on it.
plain: A tight-binding electron hops on the kagome lattice (corner-sharing triangles) in a uniform magnetic field. Is the energy spectrum a Cantor set whenever the flux per unit cell is irrational? This is known for the square lattice (Ten Martini), the honeycomb lattice and the Lieb lattice, each by a reduction to a one-dimensional operator. Isolated eigenvalues (flat bands) are set aside by taking the derived set. The analogous claim for every periodic planar network is false: in a square lattice whose vertical bonds are replaced by π-flux rhombi, Aharonov–Bohm caging gives spectral intervals.
math: Let K be the kagome lattice with unit edge length: vertices L + {(0,0),(1,0),(1/2,√3/2)}, L = ℤ(2,0)+ℤ(1,√3), edges = pairs at distance 1. For a constant field B with vector potential A let (H_Bψ)(x) = Σ_{y∼x} e^{i∫_{[x,y]}A} ψ(y) on ℓ²(V(K)), and 2πα = B·covol(L) = 2√3 B. Let Σ' be the derived set of σ(H_B). Prove or disprove: for every irrational α, Σ' is a Cantor set (nonempty, compact, perfect, nowhere dense). (The analogous statement for all periodic planar graphs is false: Aharonov–Bohm caging in a square lattice whose vertical edges are replaced by π-flux rhombi gives spectral intervals at irrational α.)

title: Do GRH and Elliott–Halberstam together refute the Alternative Hypothesis?
credit: Baluyot, Goldston, Suriajaya, Turnage-Butterbaugh, The Alternative Hypothesis for zeros of the Riemann zeta-function, arXiv:2508.10857 (2025); Goldston et al., arXiv:2507.06823; Lagarias–Rodgers arXiv:1905.12123.
premise_risks: arXiv:2508.10857 (2025 preprint, unrefereed as far as known): the problem takes its precise definition of AH, and the claimed explicit limit of F(α) under RH + AH, from this paper.
arXiv:2507.06823 (2025 preprint): background on F(α) under AH.
plain: The Alternative Hypothesis says normalized gaps between zeta zeros are almost all near half-integers. It contradicts GUE, but no proven hypothesis is known to rule it out. Decide whether GRH plus Elliott–Halberstam (strong statements about primes, not zeros) is incompatible with it.
math: Let AH be as in arXiv:2508.10857. Does RH + GRH for Dirichlet L-functions + the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture (or GEH) imply that AH fails? (The 'equivalently' clause is a research route, not an equivalent statement, and is dropped.)

title: Lower the exponent 1/2 in Pasten's subexponential abc bound
credit: Extends H. Pasten, Invent. Math. 2024 (arXiv:2312.03566), Thm 1.4.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.01327 (2026 preprint): cited in refs; M does not depend on it.
plain: Unconditionally, abc is known only in very weak forms. Pasten (2024) proved that if a ≤ c^{1−η} then log c ≤ η^{-1} exp(κ√(log R · log log R)), with R = rad(abc). abc predicts log c ≤ (1+ε) log R + O(1). Replace the square root by any smaller power of log R.
math: For coprime $a+b=c$ with $R=\mathrm{rad}(abc)$, Pasten (Invent. Math. 2024, Thm 1.4) proves: if $a\le c^{1-\eta}$ then $\log c\le \eta^{-1}\exp\big(\kappa\sqrt{\log R\,\log_2 R}\big)$; and $\log c\le q\exp(\kappa\sqrt{\log R\log_2R})$ with $q=\min\{P(a),P(b),P(c)\}$. Prove either statement with $\exp((\log R)^{\theta})$ for some fixed $\theta<1/2$, or $\exp(O(\sqrt{\log R}))$.

title: Blow-up under a steady force
credit: Fefferman, Clay Millennium problem statement (forced breakdown on R^3); OpenAI forced blow-up claim (2026, unrefereed)
premise_risks: OpenAI company PDF (cdn.openai.com navier-stokes.pdf, unrefereed): claimed time-dependent forced blow-up. This is motivation only and Claim does not depend on it.
arXiv:2609.10262 (2026 preprint): cited for context (possibly the source of the Cao-Chi-Nie gradient-force remark); Claim does not depend on it.
plain: The 2026 forced Navier–Stokes blow-up uses a push that varies in time and is switched on and off. Can a smooth, compactly supported push that never changes in time also drive a fluid at rest to a singularity?
math:
Decide whether there is $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, independent of $t$, such that the solution of $\partial_tu+(u\cdot

title: Critical NLS blow-up threshold on the cube surface
credit: Extension of Weinstein (Comm. Math. Phys. 1983) mass-critical threshold; related Strichartz work on flat cones by Ford and by Blair-Ford-Marzuola.
plain: In the plane, the focusing cubic Schrödinger equation needs at least the ground-state mass to blow up. On the surface of a cube, each corner is a cone with total angle 3π/2, which can hold a 'three-quarter' ground state. So the blow-up threshold should drop to three quarters of the planar one, and the claim is that it does exactly that.
math: Let $S$ be the surface of the unit cube with its flat metric, and let $\Delta$ be the Friedrichs extension of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\{\text{vertices}\})$. Let $Q$ be the ground state of $\Delta Q-Q+Q^3=0$ on $\mathbb R^2$, and put $m_*=\tfrac34\|Q\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}^2$. For $iu_t+\Delta u+|u|^2u=0$ on $S$, prove: (i) every $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*$ gives a global (forward-in-time) $H^1$ solution; (ii) for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $m_*<\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*+\varepsilon$ whose solution blows up in finite time (its $H^1$ norm is unbounded on its maximal interval $[0,T)$, $T<\infty$). (Stronger, optional: blow-up data exist for every mass $m>m_*$; also decide whether there is blow-up at mass exactly $m_*$.)

title: Derivative loss in L4 Strichartz on the cube surface
credit: Blair, Ford, Marzuola, Strichartz estimates for the wave equation on flat cones / Euclidean surfaces with conical singularities, arXiv:1003.0666.
results: s* >= 0 (trivial). No positive lower bound known. s* <= 1/4: Blair-Ford-Marzuola, Thm 1.5 (arXiv 1003.0666), loss 1/p for compact Euclidean surfaces with conical singularities, p=q=4; authors call the loss an artifact of the method.
plain: On the flat torus, the L4 space-time estimate for Schrodinger waves loses only epsilon derivatives (Bourgain). On the surface of a cube, which has eight cone points that diffract waves, only a loss of 1/4 derivative is known. Find the true loss: prove any loss below 1/4, or show some loss is necessary.
math: Let $S$ be the unit cube surface, $\Delta$ the Friedrichs extension from $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\text{vertices})$, and $s^*=\inf\{s\ge0:\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^4([0,1]\times S)}\le C_s\|f\|_{H^s(S)}\}$. Known: $0\le s^*\le\tfrac14$ (Blair–Ford–Marzuola). Prove $s^*<\tfrac14$, or $s^*>0$; ideally determine $s^*$ (conjecturally $0$). The board's target (Claim) is $s^*<\tfrac14$.

title: Does an oscillating source lower the Strauss exponent?
results: Bound p_c<=1+sqrt2 is correct: John/Zhou iteration uses only |F(u)|<=C|u|^p and |F(u)-F(v)|<=C(|u|+|v|)^{p-1}|u-v|, both hold for g(t)|u|^p. The 'resonance predicts 2' heuristic (exp of int t^{1-p}) is arithmetically right but not an argument; a normal-form attempt (H''=g) just recycles the oscillating factor, so nothing is proved.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.28389 (2026 preprint): cited background on Strauss-type problems with time-dependent coefficients; the statement does not depend on it.
plain: For the 3D wave equation with source |u|^p, small smooth data give global solutions exactly when p > 1+√2 (Strauss). Multiply the source by a factor that oscillates periodically in time with average zero, such as cos t. The global-existence proof still works above 1+√2. Every blow-up proof below it breaks, because they all need the source to be positive. Is the true threshold strictly smaller?
math: For u_tt − Δu = cos(t)|u|^p on R^{1+3} (continuous Kirchhoff–Duhamel mild solutions), is p_c < 1+√2, i.e. does some p in (1,1+√2) have small-data global existence for all real C_c^∞ data? Exact p_c, dependence on g and lifespan are not formalized; the all-g version is ClaimGeneral (secondary).

title: Euler with reversed stretching

plain: Flip the sign of the vortex-stretching term in the 3D Euler vorticity equation and keep advection and the Biot-Savart law. Do smooth solutions stay smooth forever, or can they blow up in finite time?

On $\mathbb T^3$ let $\omega:\mathbb T^3	imes[0,T)	o\mathbb R^3$ solve $\partial_t\omega+(u\cdot

title: Forced blow-up up to the Lions threshold
credit: OpenAI, forced Navier–Stokes blow-up (Sep 2026, unrefereed PDF); Lions (1969) for α ≥ 5/4; Tao, averaged Navier–Stokes (arXiv:1402.0290).
premise_risks: OpenAI Navier–Stokes PDF (Sep 2026, company PDF, unrefereed, reportedly Lean-formalized): the problem assumes forced blow-up from rest is known at α = 1.
arXiv:2609.10262 (2026 preprint): cited as related forced-blow-up work for the Laplacian; motivation only.
plain: With an ordinary Laplacian, a smooth compactly supported push can make a fluid at rest blow up in finite time (OpenAI, 2026). With dissipation (-Δ)^α for α ≥ 5/4, Lions proved that solutions stay smooth. Does forced blow-up from rest still happen for every α strictly between 1 and 5/4?
math:
For $\alpha\in(1,5/4)$ consider $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u+
abla p=-(-\Delta)^{\alpha}u+f$, $
abla\cdot u=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$, $u(\cdot,0)=0$. Determine the set of $\alpha\in(1,5/4)$ for which there exists $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3	imes(0,\infty);\mathbb R^3)$ whose unique smooth solution satisfies $\limsup_{t\uparrow T}\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty}=\infty$ for some $T<\infty$. In particular, is it all of $(1,5/4)$, or is it nonempty?

title: Forced Navier–Stokes blow-up at a no-slip wall
credit: Extends the OpenAI 2026 forced Navier–Stokes blow-up (cdn.openai.com navier-stokes.pdf) and Cao–Chi–Nie, arXiv:2609.10262.
premise_risks: OpenAI navier-stokes.pdf (company PDF, unrefereed): the existence of forced finite-time blow-up on R^3/T^3 from rest with C_c^infty force; motivates the problem (statement itself does not depend on it).
Cao–Chi–Nie arXiv:2609.10262 (2026 preprint): interior-ball placement of blow-up in domains; used to argue interior case is 'already available'.
Lei–Ren arXiv:2609.35406 (2026 preprint): R^3 forced blow-up; background only.
plain: In 2026 it was shown that a smooth, compactly supported force can drive the 3D Navier–Stokes equations, started from rest, to blow up in finite time. Inside a domain this can simply be copied away from any wall. Show that blow-up can also happen at the wall itself: in a half-space with the no-slip condition, the velocity becomes unbounded at a point of the boundary.
math:
Let $\mathbb R^3_+=\{x_3>0\}$, $
u>0$. Construct $f\in C^\infty_c(\overline{\mathbb R^3_+}	imes(0,\infty);\mathbb R^3)$ and a solution $(u,p)$ of $\partial_t u-
u\Delta u+(u\cdot
abla)u+
abla p=f$, $
abla\cdot u=0$ in $\mathbb R^3_+	imes(0,T)$, $u|_{x_3=0}=0$, $u(\cdot,0)=0$, with $u\in C^\infty(\overline{\mathbb R^3_+}	imes[0,T))$, $\sup_{t<T}\|u(t)\|_{L^2}<\infty$ and $\limsup_{t\uparrow T}\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty}=\infty$, such that $u$ stays bounded on $\{x_3>r\}	imes[0,T)$ for every $r>0$ (all singular points lie on the wall).

title: Heat with a cosine reaction
credit: H. Fujita 1966 (critical exponent); R. Pinsky 1997 (weighted Fujita problem, a >= 0)
plain: In u_t = u_xx + cos(x) u^2 the reaction term averages to zero over a period, but a second-order (homogenization) effect produces an effective +u^3 term, which in one dimension is exactly Fujita's borderline exponent where every positive solution of u_t = u_xx + u^3 blows up. Does every positive solution of the cosine equation blow up in finite time?
math: Let $d\ge1$, $a\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ be $\mathbb Z^d$-periodic with $\int_{[0,1]^d}a=0$, $a\not\equiv0$. Consider $u_t=\Delta u+a(x)u^p$, $u(\cdot,0)=u_0\in C_c(\mathbb R^d)$, $u_0\ge0$, $u_0\not\equiv0$. Prove: (i) if $1<p\le1+1/d$, every such solution blows up in finite time; (ii) if $p>1+1/d$, solutions with sufficiently small $u_0$ are global. Test case: $d=1$, $p=2$, $a=\cos(2\pi x)$ (equivalently $a=\cos x$ with $2\pi$-periodicity).

title: Ising spin at a cube corner
credit: Chelkak, Hongler, Izyurov, Conformal invariance of spin correlations in the planar Ising model, Ann. Math. 2015 (arXiv:1202.2838)
results: The CFT step is correct. With w=z^{4/3}, the apex spin has dimension (2pi/alpha)(1/8)=1/6, and 1/6+1/8=7/24. For alpha=2pi the formula gives back 1/4. The lattice description is right: the apex has degree 3 and axis vertices have degree 4. The beta_c value is right. The free-boundary infinite-volume limit exists by GKS monotonicity. The apex defect is irrelevant (energy dimension >0), so 7/24 should be universal.
plain: Glue three quarter-planes of the square grid into the surface of an infinite cube corner (a flat cone of angle 3π/2) and run the critical Ising model. Prove that the spin at the corner decorrelates with the exponent 7/24 predicted by conformal field theory.
math: Let $\Gamma$ be the union of the three quadrant lattices $\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2$ on the faces of $\partial\mathbb R_{\ge0}^3$, glued along the coordinate axes, with apex $o$ (degree 3; every other vertex has degree 4). Let $\langle\cdot\rangle$ be the infinite-volume limit of the nearest-neighbour Ising model at $\beta_c=\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)$ with free boundary conditions on $\Gamma\cap\{\|x\|_\infty\le n\}$. Prove $\langle\sigma_o\sigma_x\rangle\asymp|x|^{-7/24}$ as $|x|\to\infty$.

title: Alternating quotients of knot groups
credit: Dunfield-Thurston, Finite covers of random 3-manifolds, Invent. Math. 2006 (arXiv:math/0502567), question on alternating quotients; Everitt / Liebeck-Shalev for Fuchsian groups
results: Computer-verified in a fresh script: trefoil (xyx=yxy) surjects onto A5 but not A6 or A7. Figure-eight (w=x^-1yxy^-1) surjects onto A4 and A6 but not A5, A7 or A8, and has no S3 quotient, as det=5 requires. n>=9 not rerun (would take more than 30s). The trefoil argument (centre maps trivially, factor through C2*C3, Miller's (2,3)-generation) is correct.
plain: The trefoil's group maps onto every alternating group A_n with n>=9, because modulo its centre it is the modular group. Show that every nontrivial knot group maps onto A_n for all large n, or at least for infinitely many n, and bound the last exception in terms of the knot.
math: Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial knot and $G_K=\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)$. (a) Prove that $G_K$ surjects onto $A_n$ for all $n\ge N(K)$, and bound $N(K)$ in terms of the crossing number. (b) Weaker: prove that $G_K$ surjects onto $A_n$ for infinitely many $n$, or even for one $n\ge5$. Data (exhaustive search over pairs of conjugate even permutations, meridians $x,y$ with $wx=yw$): for the trefoil ($w=xy$) a surjection exists exactly for $n=5$ and $n\ge9$, since every surjection kills the centre and factors through $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)\cong C_2*C_3$, and Miller proved $(2,3)$-generation of $A_n$ for $n\ne3,6,7,8$. For the figure-eight knot ($w=x^{-1}yxy^{-1}$) a surjection exists for $n=6,9,10$ and not for $n=5,7,8$. Is $N(4_1)=9$, i.e. does $G_{4_1}$ surject onto $A_n$ for every $n\ge9$?

title: Infinitely many knot types in the symmetric ABC flow
credit: Etnyre & Ghrist (2000), arXiv:math-ph/9906021; Enciso, Peralta-Salas (and Romaniega), arXiv:2006.15033.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.17449 (Szumiński–Llibre, 2026 preprint): cited only as related perturbative work; nothing in the statement depends on it.
plain: Steady Euler flows can carry knotted streamlines, and generic high-frequency Beltrami fields on the torus contain every knot. Show that the most-studied explicit example, the ABC flow with A = B = C = 1, has closed streamlines tied in infinitely many different knots.
math: Let $X=(\sin z+\cos y,\ \sin x+\cos z,\ \sin y+\cos x)$ on $\mathbb T^3=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$ (a curl eigenfield, $\nabla\times X=X$). Prove that the periodic orbits of $X$ that lie in some embedded 3-ball $B\subset\mathbb T^3$ realize infinitely many distinct knot types (as knots in $B\cong$ a ball in $\mathbb R^3$). Stronger: every knot type is realized.

title: Order of magnitude of ex(n, C_8)
credit: Erdos; Bondy-Simonovits; Furedi-Simonovits survey.
premise_risks: Famous long-standing problem; may be judged better suited to the main set or too hard
plain: How many edges can a graph on n vertices have without containing a cycle of length 8? It is known to be at most about n^{5/4}, but the best constructions are smaller by a polynomial factor, unlike lengths 4, 6 and 10 where matching constructions exist. Find a C_8-free graph with about n^{5/4} edges, or prove a smaller upper bound.
math: Determine whether $\mathrm{ex}(n,C_8)=\Theta(n^{5/4})$. Known: $\Omega(n^{6/5})\le\mathrm{ex}(n,C_8)\le O(n^{5/4})$. (In general $\mathrm{ex}(n,C_{2k})=O(n^{1+1/k})$ by Bondy-Simonovits, with matching order known only for $k\in\{2,3,5\}$; the lower bound $n^{6/5}$ comes from generalized hexagons and equals the Lazebnik-Ustimenko-Woldar bound $n^{1+2/(3k-3+\epsilon)}$ with $k=4,\epsilon=1$.) Equivalently (given the upper bound): are there $c>0$ and $N$ such that for every $n\ge N$ some $C_8$-free graph on $n$ vertices has $\ge c\,n^{5/4}$ edges? Any exponent above $6/5$ would also be progress.
review_note: Known: Upper O(n^{5/4}): Bondy-Simonovits (1974); constants improved by Verstraete, Pikhurko, Bukh-Jiang. Lower Omega(n^{6/5}): incidence graph of a generalized hexagon (girth 12), matching Lazebnik-Ustimenko-Woldar n^{1+2/(3k-3+ε)} at k=4, ε=1; see Furedi-Simonovits, arXiv:1306.5167. Order known only for C_4, C_6, C_10 (Benson, Wenger, generalized polygons). 2026 work on C_8 (arXiv:2607.03856 generalized Turán; arXiv:2607.16103 planar Turán) does not touch the ordinary exponent.

title: An effective bound for the sum-free excess
credit: Bedert (2025) remark; Eberhard-Green-Manners (2014).
premise_risks: EGM's argument might yield a very weak explicit rate on careful bookkeeping; the (log N)^{-c} target avoids this but may be much harder
Truth could be N/3 + N^{1-c} or much smaller; no conjecture on the true rate
plain: Every set of N nonzero integers contains a sum-free subset (no x+y=z inside it) of size a bit more than N/3; Bedert (2025) showed the excess grows at least like log log N. It is also known that you cannot always beat N/3 by more than o(N), but that proof gives no rate. Prove a quantitative version: some N-element sets have no sum-free subset larger than N/3 + N/(log N)^c.
math: Let $S(N)=\min_{A\subset\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\},\,|A|=N}\max\{|B|:B\subseteq A\text{ sum-free}\}$. Known: $N/3+c\log\log N\le S(N)\le N/3+o(N)$, with the $o(N)$ ineffective. Prove that there is $c>0$ with $S(N)\le N/3+O\big(N/(\log N)^{c}\big)$. Any explicitly quantified $o(N)$ (e.g. $N/(\log\log N)^{c}$) would be partial progress.
review_note: Known: Lower: Erdos (1965) $N/3$; Alon-Kleitman $(N+1)/3$; Bourgain $(N+2)/3$; Bedert, arXiv:2502.08624 (2025) $N/3+c\log\log N$. Upper: Eberhard-Green-Manners, Annals 180 (2014), arXiv:1301.4579: $N/3+o(N)$, ineffective.

title: Does the trefoil have a symbiont?
credit: Brittenham & Hermiller, arXiv 2601.18757 (2026), Cor. 4.2 and Sec. 3/5
premise_risks: Fast-moving area: a late-2026 preprint could settle u(10_6)
Mirror conventions: the bound u(3_1#10_6) ≤ 3 is for a specific mirror pairing
u(10_6)=2 would not settle the trefoil question, since another partner could exist
plain: The unknotting number of a knot is the fewest crossing changes needed to turn it into an unknotted loop. In 2025 it was shown that tying two knots together end to end can need fewer changes than the two knots need separately, and in 2026 that every torus knot except possibly the trefoil has a partner like this. Does the trefoil, the simplest knot, also have such a partner? The most likely candidate is the 10-crossing knot 10_6, whose own unknotting number is still unknown (it is 2 or 3).
math: Write $u(K)$ for the unknotting number and $\#$ for connected sum. Knots $K,K'$ are symbionts if $u(K\#K')<u(K)+u(K')$. Is there a knot $K$, with some choice of mirror image, such that $u(3_1\#K)<1+u(K)$? By Scharlemann's theorem any such $K$ has $u(K)\ge2$. Concrete subquestion: is $u(10_6)=3$? Brittenham–Hermiller prove $u(3_1\#10_6)\le3$ for the mirror choice with $|\sigma(3_1\#10_6)|=2$, so $u(10_6)=3$ would give a positive answer.
review_note: Known: Additivity fails: $u(7_1\#\overline{7_1})\le5$ (Brittenham–Hermiller, arXiv:2506.24088, 2025). Every non-trivial torus knot except possibly $T(2,3)$ has a symbiont (Cor. 4.2), and $u(3_1\#10_6)\le3$ with $u(10_6)\in\{2,3\}$ (Thm 1.3); the paper calls deciding $u(10_6)$ an interesting open problem (Brittenham–Hermiller, arXiv:2601.18757, 2026). Scharlemann: $u(K\#K')\ge2$ for non-trivial $K,K'$. arXiv:2608.25256 (2026) obtains 194 new unknotting numbers of alternating knots with d-invariants and Owens' theorem; it began as an attempt to prove $u(10_6)=3$ and says $u(10_6)$ is still unknown. Lee (arXiv:2609.09861, 2026) also lists $10_6$ as unresolved in $[2,3]$.

title: Beat the 4-cycle lower bound for cube-free graphs
credit: P. Erdős and M. Simonovits (1970)
premise_risks: Statement is a one-sided target; the vetter may prefer the full Θ(n^{8/5}) conjecture
Erdős conjectured the n^{8/5} order, but the problem is not commonly named after a person ('Turán number of the cube'); the stated target (beat n^{3/2}) is an unnamed sub-question
plain: How many edges can an n-vertex graph have without containing the 3-dimensional cube Q3 (8 vertices, 12 edges)? Erdos and Simonovits proved about n^{8/5} is an upper bound, but the best lower bound is still about n^{3/2}, from graphs with no 4-cycle at all (every 4-cycle-free graph is cube-free). Find cube-free graphs with polynomially more edges than that, or show that no such graphs exist.
math: Let $\mathrm{ex}(n,Q_3)$ be the maximum number of edges in an $n$-vertex simple graph with no subgraph isomorphic to the cube $Q_3$. Known: $(\tfrac12+o(1))n^{3/2}\le \mathrm{ex}(n,Q_3)= O(n^{8/5})$. Decide whether $\liminf_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{\log \mathrm{ex}(n,Q_3)}{\log n}>\dfrac32$, i.e. whether there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $\mathrm{ex}(n,Q_3)\ge n^{3/2+\varepsilon}$ for all large $n$. (Erdos conjectured the stronger $\mathrm{ex}(n,Q_3)=\Theta(n^{8/5})$.)
review_note: Known: Upper: Erdős–Simonovits (1970) O(n^{8/5}); new proof by Pinchasi–Sharir and Füredi (arXiv 1307.1062). Lower: Ω(n^{3/2}) from C4-free polarity graphs, since C4 ⊂ Q3 (Erdős problems page states no better lower bound known). Janzer–Sudakov (Forum Math. Sigma, arXiv 2211.02015): ex(n,Q_d)=O(n^{2-1/(d-1)+1/((d-1)2^{d-1})}), and they record that for Q3 the bounds n^{3/2} and n^{8/5} still stand.

title: Does the variance of the LCS of two random binary strings tend to infinity?
credit: Chvatal-Sankoff (1975), Waterman (1994), Steele (1986); stated as open by Deslandes-Houdre (2024)
premise_risks: The conjectured answer (linear) is supported by simulations and analogous non-uniform theorems but not certain; an early simulation suggested much smaller fluctuations. If false, the honest problem is the order of the variance; the vetter may prefer the weaker but unconditional open target Var(L_n) -> infinity.
plain: Pick two independent uniformly random binary strings of length n and let L_n be the length of their longest common subsequence. Its mean is about 0.81n and its variance is at most n/4. Show that the variance tends to infinity, i.e. that L_n is not concentrated within a bounded window around its mean. (Linear order of the variance is believed, but even unboundedness is open.)
math: For independent uniform $X,Y\in\{0,1\}^n$ let $L_n=\mathrm{LCS}(X,Y)$. Prove that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{Var}(L_n)=\infty$. (Known: $\mathrm{Var}(L_n)\le n/4$; the stronger $\mathrm{Var}(L_n)\ge cn$ is the uniform case of Waterman's conjecture.)
review_note: Known: $\mathrm{Var}(L_n)\le n/4$ (Steele 1986 via Efron-Stein; constant from Deslandes-Houdre, arXiv 2401.03063). $\mathrm{Var}=\Theta(n)$ proved for binary letters with one letter of small probability (Lember-Matzinger, Ann. Probab. 2009, arXiv math/0702036), for 3-letter vs binary asymmetric case (Bonetto-Matzinger, arXiv math/0410404), with an omitted letter (Houdre-Ma, arXiv 1812.09552), and conditional CLT (Houdre-Islak, arXiv 1408.1559). Deslandes-Houdre (2024) prove a necessary condition for linearity in the uniform case but state 'it is still an open problem to determine whether or not, in the uniform case, the variance tends to infinity.' Simulations: Liu-Houdre (arXiv 1705.06826) fit exponent 0.91 and conjecture linear order; earlier Bonetto-Matzinger simulations suggested sd o(n^{1/3}).

title: Are random Cayley graphs of S_n expanders?
credit: Long-standing question (attributed variously to Lubotzky and to Babai); stated as open in Handel (2025)
premise_risks: Could be false (non-expansion for random generators would itself be a major surprise but is not ruled out).
Exact form of the best known inverse-polynomial gap bound after Helfgott-Seress-Zuk should be confirmed by the vetter.
plain: Pick two uniformly random permutations s, t of n symbols and run the random walk on the group they generate (with high probability all of S_n or A_n) that at each step multiplies by one of s, t, s^-1, t^-1 chosen uniformly. Is the spectral gap of this walk bounded below by a fixed positive constant, with probability tending to 1 as n grows? Specific bounded generating sets of S_n are known to give expanders, but for random generators the best proven gap still tends to 0 polynomially in n.
math: For $\sigma,\tau\in S_n$ let $H=\langle\sigma,\tau\rangle$ and $Pf(x)=\tfrac14\sum_{g\in\{\sigma^{\pm1},\tau^{\pm1}\}}f(xg)$ on $\ell^2(H)$, with second-largest eigenvalue $\lambda_2(\sigma,\tau)$ (largest eigenvalue on $\{f:\sum_x f(x)=0\}$). Prove or disprove: there is an absolute $\varepsilon>0$ such that, for $\sigma,\tau$ independent and uniform in $S_n$, $\Pr[\lambda_2(\sigma,\tau)\le 1-\varepsilon]\to1$ as $n\to\infty$.
review_note: Known: Whp $\langle\sigma,\tau\rangle\in\{A_n,S_n\}$ (Dixon 1969). Whp diameter $O(n^2(\log n)^c)$ and mixing time $O(n^3(\log n)^c)$, i.e. a gap that is only inverse polynomial (Helfgott-Seress-Zuk, J. Algebra 2015, arXiv 1311.6742); improved but still non-constant bounds later (e.g. Eberhard-Jezernik on Babai's conjecture for random generators). Random permutations have near-optimal spectral gap on $k$-tuples for $k\le n^{1/20-\epsilon}$ (Cassidy, arXiv 2412.13941), and constant $k$ earlier (Friedman et al. 1998). Some explicit bounded generating sets of $S_n$ give expanders (Kassabov, Invent. Math. 2007). No constant gap for random generators.

title: Logarithmically many conjugacy classes
