(Necessary condition, Sogge-Zelditch 2016: $M$ has a pole $p$, meaning all geodesics from $p$ return smoothly closed at a common time $2T_p$.)

title: Non-arithmetic tones of the cube
plain: Many vibration frequencies of a cube's surface come from flat tori and are rational multiples of pi squared. Prove that at least one frequency is not of this form.
math: Let $S$ be the boundary of the unit cube $[0,1]^3$ with its intrinsic flat metric (8 cone points of angle $3\pi/2$), and let $\Delta$ be the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian on $S$. Prove that some eigenvalue of $\Delta$ is not in $\pi^2\mathbb{Q}$.

title: Spikes at the primes
credit: C. R. de Oliveira and G. Q. Pellegrino, '(De)Localization in the Prime Schrodinger Operator', 2001, arXiv:cond-mat/0103313.
plain: Put a bump of fixed height at every prime on the half-line lattice and study the electron (discrete Schrodinger operator). What kind of spectrum does it have inside the free band (-2,2)? If the primes behaved like a random sparse set (Cramer model), the states would be localized (pure point spectrum); is that true for the actual primes?
math: Let $(Hu)(n)=u(n+1)+u(n-1)+\lambda\mathbf 1_{\mathbb P}(n)u(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with Dirichlet condition $u(0)=0$, $\lambda\ne0$. Determine the spectral type of $H$ on $(-2,2)$. In particular: is the spectral measure restricted to $(-2,2)$ pure point (with exponentially or sub-exponentially decaying eigenfunctions), or does it have a singular continuous part, e.g. near $E=0$?

title: Two-frequency localization
credit: Recognised open problem from the Bourgain-Goldstein / Bourgain-Goldstein-Schlag multi-frequency programme; stated open in arXiv:2603.07180 (2026). Pure point spectrum without exponential decay at fixed Diophantine frequency: Eliasson, Acta Math. 1997.
premise_risks: arXiv:2603.07180 (2026 preprint): the problem relies on its statement that it is unknown whether any fixed Diophantine frequency vector gives localization.
arXiv:2603.10649 (2026 preprint): cited background; content not relied on in the statement.
plain: Take a one-dimensional lattice Schrödinger operator whose potential is the sum of two cosines with frequencies √2 and √3, and make the coupling strong. Prove that for these specific frequencies, not just for almost every frequency pair, almost every phase gives localized eigenfunctions that decay exponentially.
math: For $\lambda>0$ and $\theta\in\mathbb T^2$ let $(H_{\lambda,\theta}\psi)(n)=\psi(n+1)+\psi(n-1)+\lambda\big(\cos2\pi(n\sqrt2+\theta_1)+\cos2\pi(n\sqrt3+\theta_2)\big)\psi(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb Z)$. Prove there is $\lambda_0$ such that for all $\lambda\ge\lambda_0$ and Lebesgue-a.e. $\theta$, $H_{\lambda,\theta}$ has pure point spectrum with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions (Anderson localization).

title: Wind-driven fire confinement threshold
credit: A. Bressan, Differential inclusions and the control of forest fires, J. Differential Equations 2007 (non-isotropic Thm 5)
results: sigma*(a,b) >= Lambda*(a-b), Lambda ~ 1.62621 (isotropic lower bound, arXiv 2610.36919, Thm 4.1). Proof: F contains the disc of radius a-b. Bressan's comparison lemma moves blocking from F to that disc, and rescaling time reduces to unit speed. sigma*(a,b) <= 2 max_{theta in [0,pi]} (a+b cos theta) sin theta (Bressan, Thm 5, non-isotropic case; applies because rho is even and nonincreasing on [0,pi]). This equals 2a at b=0 and tends to (3 sqrt3/2) a as b->a.
premise_risks: arXiv:2610.36919 (2026 preprint): isotropic lower bound Lambda ~ 1.6262 (Thm 4.1), used for the lower bound recorded in the notes.
plain: A fire spreads from a point, faster downwind: speed a + b cos(theta) in direction theta (0<=b<a). Firefighters build a barrier at speed sigma. Let sigma*(a,b) be the smallest speed that can confine the fire. Known: 1.626(a-b) <= sigma* <= 2 max (a+b cos theta) sin theta. Improve either bound, especially in the strong-wind limit b/a -> 1, where the lower bound tends to 0 but the upper bound stays near 2.6a.
math: With F_b = conv{r e^{i theta}: 0<=r<=1+b cos theta}, R_0 the open unit disc and Bressan-admissible barriers, prove that for some fixed b in (0,1) the fire can be confined with some sigma < 2 max_theta (1+b cos theta) sin theta, i.e. Bressan's anisotropic upper bound is not sharp.

title: Blank jigsaw with few edge shapes
credit: Mossel & Ross (shotgun assembly); Bordenave, Feige, Mossel 2016, arXiv:1605.03086; Nenadov, Pfister, Steger 2017, arXiv:1701.04813
plain: A jigsaw with no picture can only be solved from the shapes of its pieces. Each internal edge is one of k shapes (a tab that fits only its own matching blank), and pieces may be turned. How small can k be if some n×n blank jigsaw still goes together in exactly one way? Counting shows k must be at least about √n, and random puzzles need about n.
math: An $n\times n$ jigsaw with $k$ edge types is a map assigning to each internal edge of the $n\times n$ grid a type in $[k]$ and an orientation (which side carries the tab); border edges are flat. Its pieces are the $n^2$ unit squares, each regarded as a distinct physical object carrying its four (type, tab/blank) labels up to rotation. An assembly is a placement of all pieces bijectively on the cells, each rotated by a multiple of $90^\circ$, so that every internal edge joins a tab and a blank of the same type and all flat edges lie on the border. Let $k(n)$ be the least $k$ for which some $n\times n$ jigsaw with $k$ edge types has exactly one assembly up to the four rotations of the whole square. Determine the order of $k(n)$; in particular, is $k(n)=\Theta(\sqrt n)$?

title: Critical linear firefighter rate on Z^3
credit: Extension of Develin-Hartke (arXiv:math/0409195) and Dyer-Martinez-Pedroza-Thorne (arXiv:1507.03050, Cor. 4); o(t) failure from arXiv:2002.11205.
results: c* >= 8/243 (~0.033), elementary: Loomis-Whitney gives |vertex boundary of B| >= |B|^{2/3}; for c<2a^2-6a^3 with a=2/9, a large initial cube burns forever by induction b_t >= (a(t+T0))^3. Using the asymptotically sharp Wang-Wang vertex isoperimetry (l1-balls, constant 4(3/4)^{2/3}) the same argument heuristically gives ~32/27, not checked rigorously c* <= 8, elementary: protect the l1-sphere |x|_1=D (4D^2+2 vertices) before step D-R; c>8 suffices for large D.
plain: On the 3D grid, a finite fire spreads to all unprotected neighbours each step, and at step t you may protect about ct new vertices. It is known that linear growth is the right order. Elementary arguments show that rate c>8 always contains the fire and that c<32/27 does not. Narrow this gap, or find the exact critical rate.
math: Let c* = inf{c : for every finite initial fire B_0 ⊂ Z^3 there is a protection schedule with at most ⌊ct⌋ newly protected vertices at step t that keeps the total burnt set finite}. Elementary: the growth recursion |B_{t+1}| ≥ |B_t| + |∂B_t| − c(t+1)(t+2)/2 with the Wang–Wang vertex-isoperimetric inequality in Z^3 gives c* ≥ 32/27; numerics suggest a static wall gives c* ≲ 6.4. Target: prove c* > 32/27, i.e. some rate c > 32/27 fails to contain some finite outbreak.

title: Distinct character degrees of the symmetric group
credit: On the irreducible character degrees of symmetric groups and their multiplicities, arXiv:2410.01726 (2024)
premise_risks: arXiv:2410.01726 (preprint, refereeing status unclear): the numerical data for n <= 129 and the suggested limit near 2.5 are context only; Claim does not depend on them.
plain: Conjugate partitions always give representations of S_n of the same dimension, so at most about half of the p(n) irreducible representations can have distinct dimensions. Decide whether the fraction of distinct dimensions tends to a limit, and whether that limit is positive.
math: Let d(n) = #{f^λ : λ ⊢ n} be the number of distinct irreducible character degrees of S_n and p(n) the number of partitions of n. Prove or disprove: d(n)/p(n) converges to a positive limit L as n → ∞.

title: Is the Petersen graph common?
premise_risks: arXiv:2610.20149 (2026 preprint): cited background on common graphs; M does not depend on it.
plain: Color the edges of a huge complete graph red and blue. Does a random coloring minimize the number of single-color copies of the Petersen graph?
math: Let $P$ be the Petersen graph ($10$ vertices, $15$ edges) and $m(P)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\min_{\chi}\frac{\#\{\text{monochromatic copies of }P\text{ in }(K_n,\chi)\}}{\#\{\text{copies of }P\text{ in }K_n\}}$, minimum over red/blue colorings $\chi$ of $E(K_n)$. Is $m(P)=2^{-14}$, i.e. is $P$ common? Equivalently, is $t(P,W)+t(P,1-W)\ge 2^{-14}$ for every graphon $W$? If not, determine $m(P)$.

title: The complex of planar graphs
plain: Planar graphs on n labelled vertices form a simplicial complex, because deleting an edge keeps a graph planar. It is pure, since every maximal planar graph has 3n-6 edges. Its homology turns out not to be that of a wedge of top-dimensional spheres: already for n=6 it is concentrated two degrees lower and has 2-torsion. Determine its homology.
math: Let $\Pi_n$ be the simplicial complex on vertex set $E(K_n)$ whose faces are edge sets of planar graphs; it is pure of dimension $3n-7$. Determine $\tilde H_*(\Pi_n;\mathbb Z)$, or at least $\tilde H_*(\Pi_n;\mathbb Q)$, for all $n$. Known: $\Pi_4$ is a simplex, $\Pi_5=\partial\Delta^9\cong S^8$. For $n=6$ (computed exactly): $\tilde H_*(\Pi_6;\mathbb Q)$ is $\mathbb Q^{15}$ in degree $9=3n-9$ and $0$ elsewhere; $\tilde H_*(\Pi_6;\mathbb F_2)$ is $\mathbb F_2^{15},\mathbb F_2,\mathbb F_2$ in degrees $9,10,11$, so $\tilde H_{10}(\Pi_6;\mathbb Z)$ has $2$-torsion and $\Pi_6$ is not a wedge of spheres. The mod-2 top class is the sum of all triangulations: every face of dimension $3n-8$ of $\Pi_6$ lies in an even number (2 or 4) of facets. Questions: (a) is $\tilde H_*(\Pi_n;\mathbb Q)$ concentrated in degree $3n-9$ for all $n\ge6$, and what is its rank and $S_n$-module structure? (b) Is $\tilde H_{3n-7}(\Pi_n;\mathbb F_2)\ne0$ for all $n\ge5$? Is all torsion 2-torsion?

title: A super-constant-degree SoS integrality gap for Unique Games
credit: Barak, Sum-of-Squares open problems (lecture notes); Barak & Steurer 2014, arXiv:1404.5236
plain: Construct Unique Games instances with value <= eps on which degree-d Sum-of-Squares has value >= 1-eps, for some d = omega(1) (any slowly growing function of n), or show degree-O(1) SoS achieves a (1-eps, delta) distinguishing guarantee on all UG instances.
math: (Gap) For every eps>0 there is q=q(eps) such that for every degree D there is a Unique Games instance over [q] with optimum <= eps whose degree-2D SoS (Lasserre) value is >= 1-eps. Claim := Gap; ¬Claim is exactly the algorithmic alternative.
review_note: Context (Nov 2026): OpenAI's preprint "The Unique Games Theorem" proves UGC; together with P ≠ NP this would imply the Claim, but P ≠ NP is not known, so the Claim remains open. Context (AI-lab announcement, treated as correct): OpenAI 102: The Unique Games Conjecture and optimal approximation thresholds (The Unique Games Theorem). UGC is now a theorem (3SAT reduces to UG with completeness 1-eps, soundness delta, fixed alphabet). If not-Claim held, constant-degree SoS would decide those instances in poly time, giving P=NP. So Claim follows from P!=NP, and not-Claim would imply P=NP. It is still not proved unconditionally.
refs: Barak, Brandão, Harrow, Kelner, Steurer, Zhou, Hypercontractivity, sum-of-squares proofs, and their applications, STOC 2012, arXiv:1205.4484
Khot, Minzer, Safra, Pseudorandom sets in Grassmann graph have near-perfect expansion, FOCS 2018
Barak, Sum of Squares: open problems (lecture notes)

title: Binary-error LWE with linearly many samples
credit: Micciancio, Peikert, Hardness of SIS and LWE with small parameters, CRYPTO 2013; Arora, Ge, ICALP 2011.
plain: For LWE with secret in Z_q^n (q = poly(n)) and errors uniform in {0,1}, given m = C*n samples for a fixed constant C > 1, either give a polynomial-time (or 2^{o(n)}) algorithm, or prove hardness from standard LWE/worst-case lattice problems for m = C*n (beyond the n(1+O(1/log n)) samples of Micciancio-Peikert).
math: Fix q = q(n) with 2 <= q(n) <= poly(n) and a constant C > 1; m = ceil(Cn). Decision binary-error LWE: given (A, b), A uniform in Z_q^{m x n}, b = As + e mod q (s uniform, e uniform in {0,1}^m) or b uniform. Show that for every such C and q either (a) some randomized 2^{o(n)}-time algorithm distinguishes with non-negligible advantage, or (b) the problem is hard for polynomial time (no non-negligible advantage) assuming standard decision LWE is hard for some standard parameter family (dimension polynomially related to n, poly(n) modulus and samples, discrete Gaussian error of width alpha q' >= 2 sqrt(n')). Known: Arora-Ge solves m ~ n^2 in poly time; Micciancio-Peikert give (b) for m = n(1+O(1/log n)).
refs: Micciancio, Peikert, Hardness of SIS and LWE with small parameters, CRYPTO 2013
Arora, Ge, New algorithms for learning in presence of errors, ICALP 2011
Albrecht, Cid, Faugère, Fitzpatrick, Perret, Algebraic algorithms for LWE problems, ACM CCA 2015
Aaronson, That IACR preprint (blog post on Chen 2024), scottaaronson.blog/?p=7946

title: How fast does eps_k vanish for k-OV in low dimension?
credit: Dürr, Kipouridis, Lampis, Węgrzycki, 'Faster algorithms for k-Orthogonal Vectors in low dimension', ICALP 2026, arXiv:2507.11098; Björklund–Kaski, STOC 2024, arXiv:2310.11926.
plain: Dürr-Kipouridis-Lampis-Węgrzycki show k-OV is solvable in O(2^{(1-eps_k)d} n) for every fixed k, and that eps_k -> 0 is forced by the Set Cover Conjecture. Determine the decay rate: prove eps_k >= c/log k (or c/k), or show that eps_k >= omega(1/k) would refute the Set Cover Conjecture.
math: Prove or disprove: there are absolute constants c > 0 and p ∈ ℕ such that for every k ≥ 2, k-OV on k sets of n vectors in {0,1}^d is solvable by a deterministic word-RAM algorithm in time O_k(2^{(1 - c/ln k) d} · n^p). (The exponent p must not depend on k: otherwise brute force n^k·d makes the statement trivial. Companion SCC direction is separate.)
refs: Dürr, Kipouridis, Lampis, Węgrzycki, Faster algorithms for k-Orthogonal Vectors in low dimension, ICALP 2026, arXiv:2507.11098
Björklund, Kaski, The Asymptotic Rank Conjecture and the Set Cover Conjecture are not both true, STOC 2024, arXiv:2310.11926

title: Matching lower bound for OMv on low-VC-dimension matrices
credit: Anand, van den Brand, McCarty, 'The Structural Complexity of Matrix-Vector Multiplication', NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2502.21240; OMv conjecture: Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai, Saranurak (STOC 2015).
plain: Anand-van den Brand-McCarty give O~(n^2) preprocessing and O~(n^{2-1/d}) query time for Boolean Mv when M has VC-dimension d. Show, assuming OMv (or unconditionally in the cell-probe model), that n^{2-c/d} query time is necessary for some constant c, for d up to some omega(1) function; or improve the upper bound to n^{2-f(d)} with f(d) >> 1/d.
math: Assume the OMv conjecture (no randomized word-RAM algorithm solves OMv in total time O(n^{3-ε}) for any ε > 0). Prove there are c > 0 and D(n) → ∞ such that for every d(n) with 1 ≤ d(n) ≤ D(n), every ε > 0 and every p, no randomized algorithm with O(n^p) preprocessing answers the n online Boolean matrix-vector queries for n×n matrices of VC-dimension ≤ d(n) in total query time O(n^{3-c/d(n)-ε}) (amortized n^{2-c/d(n)-ε} per query). (Positive alternative is a separate question.)
refs: Anand, van den Brand, McCarty, The Structural Complexity of Matrix-Vector Multiplication, NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2502.21240
Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai, Saranurak, Unifying and strengthening hardness for dynamic problems via the OMv conjecture, STOC 2015

title: From density to Kolmogorov typicality of positive entropy in symplectic families
credit: P. Berger and D. Turaev, arXiv:2507.11375 (2025), Thm B; P. Berger, arXiv:2003.09329 (Kolmogorov typicality / emergence).
premise_risks: arXiv:2507.11375 (Berger-Turaev, 2025 preprint, refereeing status unverified): the problem assumes its Thm B (density of families with positive metric entropy at every parameter) and borrows its definition of Kolmogorov typicality.
plain: Berger and Turaev showed that families of area-preserving surface maps having positive metric entropy at every parameter are dense among smooth families. Show this is typical, i.e. holds for a Kolmogorov-generic (prevalent) set of families, or find a robust obstruction.
math: Take Σ = 𝕋² = ℝ²/ℤ² with the standard area form. For k ≥ 1 let 𝓕_k be the space of C^∞ families (f_p)_{p∈[0,1]^k} of symplectic diffeomorphisms of 𝕋² such that every f_p has an elliptic periodic point, with the C^∞ topology on (p,x) ↦ f_p(x), and 𝓕_+ = {families with h_Leb(f_p) > 0 for Lebesgue-a.e. p}. Prove or disprove: for every k ≥ 1, 𝓕_+ contains a countable intersection of open subsets dense in 𝓕_k (Kolmogorov typicality in the sense of Berger–Turaev). ¬Claim: for some k, 𝓕_+ contains no residual subset of 𝓕_k.

title: Integrability of the egg-crate torus
credit: V. V. Kozlov, non-integrability of perturbed geodesic flows on the torus (Poincaré-Kozlov theory; 'Symmetries, Topology and Resonances in Hamiltonian Mechanics', 1996); Paternain, Taimanov for entropy obstructions
plain: Put the surface z = ε sin x sin y over a flat square torus. Show its geodesic flow is never integrable, however small the bumps are.
math: For $\varepsilon>0$ let $g_\varepsilon$ be the metric on $\mathbb T^2=\mathbb R^2/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^2$ induced from the graph $z=\varepsilon\sin x\sin y$, i.e. $g_\varepsilon=dx^2+dy^2+\varepsilon^2(\cos x\sin y\,dx+\sin x\cos y\,dy)^2$. Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ the geodesic flow on $T^*\mathbb T^2\setminus0$ has no real-analytic first integral functionally independent of the Hamiltonian (for example, by showing positive topological entropy).

title: Positive metric entropy for the x^4+y^4 billiard
credit: O. Knill et al., billiards in l^p unit balls (lpbilliards.pdf, Harvard); positive metric entropy for smooth convex billiards / standard-map-type problem (classical open problem)
plain: The billiard table x^4 + y^4 <= 1 is smooth and convex, but its curvature vanishes at four points, so (by Mather) it has no caustics. Its phase space mixes stable islands with apparently chaotic regions. Prove that the chaos is real: on a set of positive measure, nearby trajectories separate exponentially fast.
math:
Let $\Phi$ be the billiard map of $\Omega=\{x^4+y^4\le1\}$, preserving the Liouville measure $
u=\sin	heta\,ds\,d	heta$. Prove that $h_
u(\Phi)>0$; equivalently, by Pesin's formula, that $\Phi$ has a nonzero Lyapunov exponent on a set of positive $
u$-measure.

title: Three identical vortices on a square torus are chaotic
credit: Borisov, Mamaev, Kilin, Regul. Chaotic Dyn. (2019); survey arXiv:2003.00716 (Thm 7); Stremler-Aref (1999, chao-dyn/9907038) for the zero-circulation integrable case
plain: On a flat torus, three point vortices with total circulation zero form an integrable system (Stremler-Aref), but for vortices of equal strength even three are believed chaotic, from numerics only. Prove that three identical point vortices on the square torus are not integrable; the same question is open for four.
math: For N = 3 the reduced flow on M_3 has no real-analytic first integral functionally independent of H (Claim); the N = 4 analogue is a separate proposition ClaimN4, not part of Claim.

title: Cross-polytopes in 4D
credit: Klee & Wagon, Old and New Unsolved Problems in Plane Geometry and Number Theory (1991), Problem 11.5; V. V. Makeev (d = 3); R. Karasev, arXiv:0905.2671 (2009).
plain: Every smooth convex body in 4-space should have the eight corners of a regular cross-polytope lying on its boundary.
math: Prove that for every smooth convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^4$ there is a regular cross-polytope (a similar copy of $\mathrm{conv}\{\pm e_1,\dots,\pm e_4\}$) all of whose 8 vertices lie on $\partial K$.

title: Geodesic squares on convex surfaces
credit: Toeplitz 1911 (square peg problem); Schnirelmann 1944 (smooth case); constant-curvature surfaces: arXiv:2507.07945 (Naseri Sadr 2025)
premise_risks: arXiv:2507.07945 (2025 preprint, refereeing unclear): results for spheres and the hyperbolic plane; context only, Claim does not depend on it.
plain: On a smooth convex surface, measure distance by the length of the shortest path on the surface. Every smooth simple closed curve on the surface should contain four points that form a 'square' in this sense: four equal sides and two equal diagonals.
math: Let $S=\partial K$ for a convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ with smooth boundary and positive Gaussian curvature, and let $d$ be the intrinsic distance on $S$. Prove that every smooth simple closed curve $\gamma\subset S$ contains four distinct points $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$, in this cyclic order along $\gamma$, with $d(p_1,p_2)=d(p_2,p_3)=d(p_3,p_4)=d(p_4,p_1)>0$ and $d(p_1,p_3)=d(p_2,p_4)$.

title: Sofa stability
credit: Baek (2024), 'Optimality of Gerver's Sofa', arXiv:2411.19826.
premise_risks: arXiv:2411.19826 (Baek 2024; refereeing status unclear): the problem assumes Gerver's sofa is the maximizer. The formal Claim avoids this by quantifying over an unspecified stable sofa G, so it does not depend on Baek's result.
arXiv:2610.13955 (2026 preprint, cited in refs): context only; nothing in the statement depends on it.
plain: Baek (2024) proved that Gerver's sofa has the largest area among shapes that can be moved around a right-angled corner in a hallway of width 1. Show that any movable sofa whose area is nearly Gerver's must be nearly Gerver's sofa in shape (which in particular gives uniqueness).
math: A moving sofa is a compact connected $S\subset\mathbb R^2$ that can be moved by a continuous rigid motion from $(-\infty,0]\times[0,1]$ to $[0,1]\times(-\infty,0]$ inside $L=((-\infty,1]\times[0,1])\cup([0,1]\times(-\infty,1])$. Let $G$ be Gerver's sofa, of area $A_G\approx2.21953$. Prove that there are $C,\alpha>0$ such that every moving sofa $S$ with $|S|\ge A_G-\varepsilon$ satisfies $\min_{g}|gS\,\triangle\,G|\le C\varepsilon^{\alpha}$, the minimum over rigid motions $g$ of the plane.

title: Graceful labellings of forests
credit: Relaxation of the Ringel–Kotzig–Rosa Graceful Tree Conjecture; related: Van Bussel (EJC 2002, range-relaxed graceful labellings), Adamaszek–Allen–Grosu–Hladký arXiv:1608.01577, gracesize arXiv:2511.11331.
plain: A forest with m edges and c trees has m + c vertices. Label them with 0, 1, ..., m + c - 1, each label used once, so that the m edge differences |label(u) - label(v)| are all different. Show that every forest has such a labelling. The case 'a tree plus one isolated vertex' already says that every tree can be labelled gracefully if one spare label is allowed.
math: Prove that every forest $F$ with $m$ edges and $c\ge1$ components has a bijection $\ell:V(F)\to\{0,1,\dots,m+c-1\}$ such that the values $|\ell(u)-\ell(v)|$, $uv\in E(F)$, are pairwise distinct. (Key special case: $F=T\sqcup K_1$, i.e. every tree with $m$ edges has an injective labelling into $\{0,\dots,m+1\}$ with distinct edge differences.)

title: First-order convergence law for random Latin squares
results: Caution: route (i) as originally proposed has a flaw. The extension property 'every finite partial configuration extends in every consistent way w.h.p.' is false. A new x with x∘a1=b1 and x∘a2=b2 has expected count n·n^{-2}→0, because x∘a=b already determines x. The structure is functionally sparse (Lynch-type), not G(n,1/2)-type, so the route was rewritten.
premise_risks: arXiv:2606.18174 (Allsop-Morris, 2026 preprint): cited only as evidence that even the Poisson(1) idempotent law is unproved; the statement assumes nothing from it.
plain: Pick a Latin square of order n uniformly at random and read it as a multiplication table x∘y on n symbols. Does every first-order statement about this table have a limiting probability as n grows? A zero-one law fails: the number of x with x∘x=x should be asymptotically Poisson(1), so the probability that one exists should tend to 1−1/e rather than 0 or 1.
math: Let $L_n$ be uniform among Latin squares on $[n]$ and $\mathcal Q_n=([n],\circ)$ with $x\circ y=L_n(x,y)$. Prove or disprove: for every first-order sentence $\varphi$ in the language $\{\circ,=\}$, $\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr[\mathcal Q_n\models\varphi]$ exists. (A 0-1 law should fail: by symbol-relabelling symmetry, $\mathbb E\#\{x:x\circ x=x\}=1$ exactly, and this count is conjecturally Poisson(1).) Expected route, as for Lynch's random unary functions: (i) w.h.p. the bounded-depth term closure of any bounded tuple is free except for coincidences counted by balanced configurations ($v$ elements, $v$ independent equations); (ii) a joint Poisson limit for the counts of all such balanced configurations, e.g. cycles of $x\mapsto x\circ x$. A disproof would need a definable sparse statistic with no limit law.

title: Hat Ising universality
credit: Hat tiling: Smith, Myers, Kaplan, Goodman-Strauss (2023); numerics on hat-tiling Ising models as cited in the notes (arXiv:2402.11331, arXiv:2307.11054); background: Chelkak-Smirnov universality on isoradial graphs.
plain: Magnets on a hat tiling should behave at their critical point exactly like magnets on a square grid. Prove it.
math: Let T be any hat tiling (tiling of ℂ by isometric copies, reflections allowed, of the Smith–Myers–Kaplan–Goodman-Strauss hat; all such tilings form the hull) and G its tile-adjacency graph (tiles sharing a boundary segment), with the J=1 ferromagnetic Ising model. Prove: there is β_c ∈ (0,∞), the same for all T, such that, with constants c, C, δ > 0 depending only on T: (a) the plus-state magnetization M_T(β,x) = 0 for all tiles x and 0 ≤ β ≤ β_c, and c(β−β_c)^{1/8} ≤ M_T(β,x) ≤ C(β−β_c)^{1/8} uniformly in x for β_c < β < β_c+δ; (b) for β_c−δ < β < β_c, χ_T(β) = sup_x Σ_y ⟨σ_xσ_y⟩_β satisfies c(β_c−β)^{−7/4} ≤ χ_T(β) ≤ C(β_c−β)^{−7/4}; (c) for β_c−δ < β < β_c, the inverse correlation length 1/ξ_T(β) = liminf_{|x−y|→∞} (−log⟨σ_xσ_y⟩_β/|x−y|) satisfies c(β_c−β) ≤ 1/ξ_T(β) ≤ C(β_c−β).

title: Irrationality of the quartic oscillator ground state
plain: The lowest energy of the quartic oscillator, -d^2/dx^2 + x^4 on the line, is about 1.0603620905. Show that it is irrational.
math: Let $E_0=\min\sigma\big(-\tfrac{d^2}{dx^2}+x^4\big)$, the operator taken self-adjoint on $L^2(\mathbb R)$ ($E_0=1.06036209048418\ldots$). Prove that $E_0\notin\mathbb Q$.

title: Break the 5/8 barrier for primes with triply well-factorable weights
credit: A. Pascadi, arXiv:2505.00653 (2025), Thm 1.3 and remarks on the 5/8 limit; J. D. Lichtman, arXiv:2309.08522 (2023); triply well-factorable weights from Maynard's equidistribution papers.
premise_risks: arXiv:2505.00653 (Pascadi, 2025 preprint, refereeing status unverified): the known baseline θ* ≥ 5/8 unconditionally and the exact definition of triply well-factorable weights (Def 1.1) are taken from it.
arXiv:2602.20917 and arXiv:2608.13299 (2026 preprints): used only to check that no one has passed 5/8; the statement assumes nothing from them.
plain: The primes are known to be evenly spread over residue classes, on average over moduli up to x^{5/8}, if the average is weighted by triply well-factorable weights. Push the exponent past 5/8, or show the dispersion method cannot.
math: Say (lambda_q)_{q<=Q} is triply well-factorable of level Q if for all Q1Q2Q3=Q there are 1-bounded alpha,beta,gamma supported on q_i<=Q_i with lambda=alpha*beta*gamma (Dirichlet convolution). Let theta* = sup of theta such that for all eps,A>0, fixed a!=0, and every such lambda of level Q=x^{theta-eps}: sum_{q<=Q,(q,a)=1} lambda_q(pi(x;q,a)-pi(x)/phi(q)) <<_{eps,A,a} x(log x)^{-A}. Known theta*>=5/8 (Pascadi). Prove theta*>5/8.

title: Close the gap in the density of integers that are sums of two rational cubes
credit: Alpöge, Bhargava, Shnidman, Integers expressible as the sum of two rational cubes, arXiv:2210.10730 (2022); Koymans-Smith arXiv:2606.06024 (2026) for the complement side.
premise_risks: arXiv:2606.06024 (Koymans-Smith, 2026 preprint): source of the 31.95% (0.3195) lower bound for non-sums; the formalized Claim does not use it, but the stated M does.
plain: BSD plus the minimalist rank heuristic predict that exactly half of all integers are sums of two rational cubes. Proven: at least 2/21 are (Alpöge–Bhargava–Shnidman), and at least 31.95% are not (Koymans–Smith). Improve either bound.
math: Let $\mathcal S=\{n\in\mathbb Z: n=x^3+y^3,\ x,y\in\mathbb Q\}$ and $d_\pm$ the lower densities of $\mathcal S$ and of its complement (ordered by $|n|$). Known: $\underline d(\mathcal S)\ge 2/21$, $\underline d(\mathcal S^c)\ge 0.3195$. Conjecture: both densities equal $1/2$. Improve either constant.

title: Improve H_1 <= 12 under EH alone
credit: D.H.J. Polymath 2014, arXiv:1407.4897; J. Maynard 2015, arXiv:1311.4600
plain: Assuming Elliott–Halberstam, Maynard's sieve gives infinitely many pairs of primes at distance at most 12. The generalized conjecture GEH gives 6. Lower 12 using EH alone.
math: Let $H_1=\liminf_{n}(p_{n+1}-p_n)$. Assuming EH (level $\theta=1-\varepsilon$ for all $\varepsilon>0$, for the von Mangoldt function only, not GEH), prove $H_1\le 10$, or prove that no Selberg/Maynard-type sieve weight using EH alone can give $H_1<12$.

title: Interval-sieve extremal bounds behind the Banks–Ford–Tao gap prediction
credit: Banks, Ford, Tao, Large prime gaps and probabilistic models, Invent. Math. 2023 (arXiv:1908.08613)
plain: Banks, Ford and Tao showed that a random sieve model of the primes predicts the largest prime gap below x is about g(ξ log²x), where g is controlled by an extremal sieve quantity W_y. W_y is the fewest survivors in [0,y] after one residue class is removed for each prime up to √(y/log y). Narrow the bounds on W_y.
math: Let W_y = min over residue choices (a_p) of #{n ∈ [0,y] ∩ ℤ : n ≢ a_p (mod p) for all primes p <= (y/log y)^{1/2}}. Known (Banks-Ford-Tao): (4+o(1)) y log log y/log^2 y <= W_y <= y/log y + O(y log log y/log^2 y). Prove or disprove: there is an absolute c > 0 with W_y >= c·y/log y for all sufficiently large y.

title: Largest prime factor of Markov numbers
credit: Extends Corvaja–Zannier, 'On the greatest prime factor of Markov pairs', Rend. Sem. Mat. Univ. Padova 116 (2006).
plain: Markov numbers are the numbers appearing in positive integer solutions of x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz. Show that the largest prime factor of a Markov number tends to infinity. Equivalently, for any finite set of primes, only finitely many Markov numbers are built from those primes alone.
math: Let $\mathcal M=\{m\ge1:\exists\,x,y\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\ x^2+y^2+m^2=3xym\}$ and let $P(m)$ denote the largest prime factor of $m$ (with $P(1)=1$). Prove that $P(m)\to\infty$ as $m\to\infty$ in $\mathcal M$; equivalently, for every finite set $S$ of primes, only finitely many $m\in\mathcal M$ are $S$-units.

title: Lower the exponent 0.7785 for A4-quartic fields
credit: Bhargava, Shankar, Taniguchi, Thorne, Tsimerman, Zhao, 'Bounds on 2-torsion in class groups of number fields and integral points on elliptic curves', JAMS 2020 (arXiv:1701.02458, Thm 1.4); Loughran-Paterson arXiv:2510.05248
premise_risks: arXiv:2510.05248 (Loughran-Paterson, 2025 preprint): lower bound X^{1/2} log X and the statement that 0.7784... is the current record; the Claim itself depends only on the refereed BSTTTZ exponent.
arXiv:2602.23619 (Alberts-Bucur, 2026 preprint): cited only for the status 'no 2026 improvement'.
plain: Malle predicts about X^{1/2} log X quartic fields with Galois group A4 and discriminant up to X. Loughran–Paterson (2025) proved the matching lower bound. The best upper bound is still about X^{0.7785}. Lower the exponent.
math: Let N_{A4}(X) count quartic L/Q with Gal(L~/Q)=A4 and |Delta_L|<=X. Known: X^{1/2} log X << N_{A4}(X) << X^{0.7784...+eps} (Loughran-Paterson arXiv:2510.05248 Thm 1.1; BSTTTZ JAMS 2020 Thm 1.4). Prove N_{A4}(X) << X^{beta} for some beta<0.7784 (ideally beta=1/2+eps).

title: One-level density of quadratic Dirichlet L-functions beyond support (−2,2)
credit: Özlük–Snyder (Canad. J. Math. 58, 2006; earlier 1999 work) and Rubinstein (Duke 2001) for support (−2,2); Katz–Sarnak (1999) density conjectures.
plain: Under GRH, the low-lying zeros of L(s,χ_d) for quadratic characters are known to follow the symplectic random-matrix law only for test functions whose Fourier transform is supported in (−2,2). Go beyond 2.
math: For the family of real primitive characters $\chi_{8d}$, $d$ odd squarefree, $X<d\le 2X$, and even Schwartz $\phi$ with $\operatorname{supp}\hat\phi\subset(-\sigma,\sigma)$, prove under GRH that $\frac1{|\mathcal F|}\sum_d\sum_{\gamma_d}\phi\!\big(\gamma_d\frac{\log X}{2\pi}\big)\to\int\phi(x)\big(1-\frac{\sin 2\pi x}{2\pi x}\big)dx$ for some $\sigma>2$.

title: Push the GRH lower bound for Montgomery's F(alpha) beyond alpha = 1
credit: Goldston, Gonek, Özlük, Snyder (2000), 'On the pair correlation of zeros of the Riemann zeta-function', Proc. London Math. Soc.
plain: Montgomery's function F(α) is known only for |α|≤1 (on RH). Under GRH for Dirichlet L-functions, Goldston–Gonek–Özlük–Snyder proved F(α) ≥ 3/2−|α|−ε on 1≤|α|≤3/2, while the conjecture says F(α)=1 there. Improve this lower bound.
math: Assume GRH for all Dirichlet $L$-functions. Prove that for some $\delta>0$ and all $\alpha\in[1,1+\delta]$, $\liminf_{T\to\infty}F(\alpha,T)\ge \tfrac32-\alpha+\delta$, or prove $\liminf_T \int_{1}^{3/2}F(\alpha,T)\,d\alpha>1/8$ (the value forced by the GGOS bound).

title: Second moment of 3-torsion in imaginary quadratic class groups
credit: Cohen, Lenstra, 'Heuristics on class groups of number fields', LNM 1068 (1984); Davenport-Heilbronn (1971) for the first moment
plain: Davenport–Heilbronn showed the average of |Cl(K)[3]| over imaginary quadratic fields is 2, as Cohen–Lenstra predicts. Cohen–Lenstra also predict the average of |Cl(K)[3]|² is 6. Prove this, or at least that the average is bounded.
math: Let $K$ range over imaginary quadratic fields with $|D_K|<X$. Cohen–Lenstra ($\mathbb E\,\#\mathrm{Sur}(\mathrm{Cl}_K,H)=1$ for $H=(\mathbb Z/3)^2$) predict $\frac{1}{\#\{K\}}\sum_K|\mathrm{Cl}_K[3]|^2\to 6$. Prove this limit, or prove $\sum_K|\mathrm{Cl}_K[3]|^2\ll X$.

title: A Jörgens theorem for the Hessian permanent
plain: Jörgens proved that a convex function on the whole plane whose Hessian determinant is 1 must be a quadratic polynomial. Replace the determinant by the permanent, u_xx·u_yy + u_xy², and ask whether the same rigidity holds for solutions on the elliptic branch.
math: Let $u\in C^4(\mathbb R^2)$ satisfy $u_{xx}u_{yy}+u_{xy}^2=1$, $u_{xx}>0$ and $2u_{xy}^2<1$ on $\mathbb R^2$ (these are exactly the conditions for the linearized operator $u_{yy}\partial_{xx}+2u_{xy}\partial_{xy}+u_{xx}\partial_{yy}$ to be elliptic; they force $u$ convex with $0<\det D^2u=1-2u_{xy}^2\le1$). Prove or disprove that $u$ is a quadratic polynomial.

title: KdV with a cosine coefficient
plain: Put a cos x in front of the cubic term of the modified KdV equation on the circle. The energy and the mean are still conserved, but the L² norm is not, and the energy no longer has a definite sign. Can smooth solutions blow up in finite time?
math: Consider $u_t+u_{xxx}+(\cos(x)\,u^3)_x=0$ on $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$ with real $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)$. It is Hamiltonian, $u_t=\partial_x\frac{\delta H}{\delta u}$ with $H=\int(\tfrac12u_x^2-\tfrac14\cos(x)u^4)$, and conserves $\int u$ and $H$. However, $\frac{d}{dt}\int u^2=\frac12\int\sin(x)u^4$. Decide whether every such $u_0$ yields a global smooth solution, or whether $\|u(t)\|_{H^1}\to\infty$ in finite time for some $u_0$.

title: Liouville theorem for Lane-Emden with a shifted nonlinearity
plain: Gidas-Spruck: -Delta u = u^p has no positive solution on R^n for subcritical p. Replace u^p by the value of u^p at a shifted point x+e. Is there still no positive solution, for every subcritical p?
math: Let $n\ge3$, $1<p<\frac{n+2}{n-2}$, $e\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. Prove or disprove: there is no positive $u\in C^2(\mathbb R^n)$ with $-\Delta u(x)=u(x+e)^p$ for all $x$. (For $1<p<\frac n{n-2}$ the standard Mitidieri–Pohozaev test-function argument applies, since the shift is negligible at large scales; the open range is $\frac n{n-2}\le p<\frac{n+2}{n-2}$. One may also ask whether positive solutions exist for $p\ge\frac{n+2}{n-2}$.)

title: Mass-critical scattering on flat cones
credit: B. Dodson, global well-posedness and scattering for the defocusing L^2-critical NLS in d=2 (Duke Math. J. 2016)
results: Both trivial cases check out. For alpha=2pi/k, C_alpha=R^2/Z_k: the Friedrichs modes e^{ikmθ} with Bessel order k|m| match the Z_k-invariant plane functions, and Dodson applies for any mass, with mass scaled by k. For radial data the m=0 mode on the cone is the 2D radial Laplacian. The sign convention iu_t+Δu=+|u|^2u is defocusing.
plain: Dodson proved that the defocusing cubic Schrodinger equation in the plane scatters for every finite-mass initial state. Prove the same on every flat cone, a plane with a single conical singularity of total angle alpha. For alpha = 2pi/k it follows from Dodson by symmetry, and radial data are also easy. Every other angle, such as the surface of a cube corner (alpha = 3pi/2) or alpha > 2pi, is open.
math: For $\alpha>0$ let $\mathcal C_\alpha=(0,\infty)\times(\mathbb R/\alpha\mathbb Z)$ with metric $dr^2+r^2d\theta^2$ and $\Delta$ the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian on $C_c^\infty(\mathcal C_\alpha)$. Prove that for every $\alpha>0$ and every $u_0\in L^2(\mathcal C_\alpha)$ the solution of $iu_t+\Delta u=|u|^2u$, $u(0)=u_0$, is global with $\|u\|_{L^4_{t,x}(\mathbb R\times\mathcal C_\alpha)}<\infty$, hence scatters in $L^2$. (Known: $\alpha=2\pi/k$, since $\mathcal C_{2\pi/k}=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z_k$ and Dodson applies to $\mathbb Z_k$-invariant data. Radial data for any $\alpha$, since the radial equation coincides with the 2D one.)

title: Quintic Szego growth
credit: Gérard–Grellier (cubic Szegő equation, turbulent solutions); Thirouin, quadratic Szegő equation (arXiv:1710.01512).
plain: The cubic Szego equation on the circle is completely integrable, and Gerard-Grellier showed that its smooth solutions can have Sobolev norms that are unbounded in time. Decide whether the quintic Szego equation, which is presumably not integrable, also has smooth solutions with unbounded high Sobolev norms.
math: On $L^2_+(\mathbb T)=\{u\in L^2:\hat u(k)=0\ \forall k<0\}$ with Szego projector $\Pi$, consider $i\partial_tu=\Pi(|u|^4u)$, which is globally well posed in $H^s_+$, $s>1/2$, with conserved $\|u\|_{L^2}$, $(Du,u)$ and $\|u\|_{L^6}$. Decide whether there exist $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)\cap L^2_+$ and $s>1/2$ with $\limsup_{t\to\infty}\|u(t)\|_{H^s}=\infty$.

title: Knotted billiards in a regular tetrahedron
credit: Extends Jones–Przytycki (Lissajous knots and billiard knots, 1998) and Koseleff–Pecker, 'Every knot is a billiard knot', arXiv:1106.5600; periodic orbits in polyhedra: Bedaride–Rao arXiv:1104.1051.
plain: A billiard ball bouncing periodically inside a regular tetrahedron, without hitting edges or corners, traces a closed polygon in space. Is any such polygon knotted, and do infinitely many different knot types occur?
math: Call a periodic billiard trajectory in a regular tetrahedron $T\subset\mathbb R^3$ admissible if it never meets an edge or vertex of $T$ and its image is an embedded closed polygon. (a) Does some admissible trajectory form a nontrivial knot? (b) Prove that the set of knot types of admissible periodic trajectories is infinite.

title: Does the self-avoiding-walk growth ratio converge on the square lattice?
credit: Open problem stated in Madras-Slade, The Self-Avoiding Walk (1993) and Bauerschmidt, Duminil-Copin, Goodman, Slade, Lectures on Self-Avoiding Walks (2012), Sec. 1.3.
premise_risks: Well known to specialists, so novelty is modest
Could conceivably be equivalent in difficulty to proving existence of gamma
plain: Let c_n be the number of n-step walks on the square grid that start at the origin and never visit a point twice. It is classical that c_n^{1/n} tends to a constant mu (about 2.638), and Kesten proved in 1963 that the two-step ratio c_{n+2}/c_n tends to mu^2. Does the one-step ratio c_{n+1}/c_n converge (necessarily to mu)? Numerically the ratios alternate between even and odd n with a shrinking gap, but no proof exists in dimensions 2, 3 or 4.
math: Let $c_n=\#\{(\omega_0,\dots,\omega_n)\in(\mathbb Z^2)^{n+1}:\omega_0=0,\ \|\omega_{i+1}-\omega_i\|_1=1,\ \omega_i\neq\omega_j\ (i\neq j)\}$ and $\mu=\lim_n c_n^{1/n}$. Prove that $\lim_{n\to\infty} c_{n+1}/c_n$ exists. (Given Kesten's theorem $c_{n+2}/c_n\to\mu^2$, this is equivalent to $c_{n+1}/c_n\to\mu$, i.e. to the even and odd subsequences of $c_{n+1}/c_n$ having the same limit.)

title: Planar self-avoiding walk spreads at least diffusively
credit: Madras & Slade, The Self-Avoiding Walk (1993); Bauerschmidt, Duminil-Copin, Goodman, Slade, Lectures on Self-Avoiding Walks (2012), Sec. 1.5.2.
premise_risks: Schmidt-Sellke (Feb 2026, unrefereed) technique for self-repelling walks might extend; check before posting
Low novelty: well-known open problem among SAW specialists
plain: Pick one of the self-avoiding n-step walks on the square grid from the origin uniformly at random, and let R_n^2 be the average squared distance of its endpoint from the origin. Intuition says avoiding yourself only pushes you outward, so R_n^2 should be at least of order n, the value for ordinary random walk; physicists expect n^{3/2}. Yet nobody can prove even R_n^2 >= c n for some c > 0: the best proven lower bound is of order n^{2/3}.
math: Let $\mathrm{SAW}_n$ be the set of $n$-step self-avoiding walks on $\mathbb Z^2$ starting at $0$ and $\langle|\omega(n)|^2\rangle_n=|\mathrm{SAW}_n|^{-1}\sum_{\omega\in\mathrm{SAW}_n}\|\omega_n\|_2^2$. Prove $\liminf_{n\to\infty}\langle|\omega(n)|^2\rangle_n/n>0$, equivalently: there is $c>0$ with $\langle|\omega(n)|^2\rangle_n\ge c\,n$ for all $n\ge1$.

title: Rotor-router discs: logarithmic outer error
credit: Propp's roundness question; inner/outer bounds and constant-error question from Levine & Peres (2009). The specific O(log r) outer target is my framing as the natural matching step.
premise_risks: Target O(log r) is my framing; literature frames the question as constant error
Initial rotor configuration matters for the exact statement
plain: Release n chips one at a time at the origin of the square grid. Each grid point has an arrow, all initially pointing east. A chip at an occupied point turns that point's arrow a quarter turn counterclockwise and steps the way it now points, and it stops at the first empty point. The n occupied points form a strikingly round disc of radius about r = sqrt(n/pi): simulations up to about 7*10^10 chips show inner and outer radii differing by less than 1.7. It is proved that no hole lies deeper than C log r inside the circle, but the best bound for outward bulges is about sqrt(r) log r. Prove that no occupied point lies beyond r + C log r.
math: Rotor-router aggregation on $\mathbb Z^2$: rotors $\rho:\mathbb Z^2\to\{E,N,W,S\}$ start identically $E$; chips are added one at a time at $0$; a chip at an occupied site advances that site's rotor one step counterclockwise ($E\to N\to W\to S\to E$) and moves one lattice step in the new direction, stopping at the first unoccupied site it reaches. Let $A_n$ be the set of occupied sites after $n$ chips and $r=\sqrt{n/\pi}$. Prove that there is a constant $C$ with $A_n\subseteq\{z\in\mathbb Z^2:\|z\|_2\le r+C\log(2+r)\}$ for all $n\ge1$. (Levine-Peres prove $\{z:\|z\|_2\le r-C\log(2+r)\}\cap\mathbb Z^2\subseteq A_n$ and $A_n\subseteq\{\|z\|_2\le r+C\sqrt r\log(2+r)\}$ for every initial rotor configuration.)

title: Square-lattice polygon counts satisfy no polynomial recurrence
credit: Guttmann-Enting solvability criterion; open question recorded by Rechnitzer (2006).
premise_risks: May be very hard (essentially requires structural control of an unsolved model)
Formalizing 'polygon modulo translation' needs care (cyclic, unoriented, rooted at lexicographically least vertex)
plain: Let p_n count closed self-avoiding loops of length 2n on the square grid, up to translation (p_2 = 1, p_3 = 2, p_4 = 7, p_5 = 28, ...). Many solved lattice models have counting sequences that obey a linear recurrence with polynomial coefficients (their generating function is 'D-finite'). For square-lattice polygons it is believed that no such recurrence exists, reflecting that the model has no exact solution of this kind. Prove it.
math: Let $p_n$ be the number of self-avoiding polygons (unrooted, unoriented closed nearest-neighbour cycles) of perimeter $2n$ on $\mathbb Z^2$, counted modulo translation, so $p_1=0$, $p_2=1,p_3=2,p_4=7$. Prove that there are no $k\ge0$ and polynomials $Q_0,\dots,Q_k\in\mathbb Q[x]$, not all zero, with $\sum_{i=0}^k Q_i(n)\,p_{n+i}=0$ for all $n\ge1$. Equivalently, $P(x)=\sum_n p_nx^n$ is not D-finite.

title: Does a Moore graph of degree 57 exist?
credit: Hoffman and Singleton (1960); recent restrictions by Mačaj–Širáň, Smith–Montemanni, and others
premise_risks: Very famous problem: low novelty, high difficulty
'Moore graph' is a person-named object, but the question is not a named conjecture
Two 2026 partial-result papers are recent (one arXiv only); they do not affect the open status
plain: A Moore graph of diameter 2 is a regular graph in which any two vertices are either adjacent or have exactly one common neighbour; with degree k it has k^2+1 vertices, the most a diameter-2 graph of degree k can have. Hoffman and Singleton (1960) showed such graphs can exist only for k = 2, 3, 7, 57, and the first three exist (pentagon, Petersen graph, Hoffman-Singleton graph). Does one exist for degree 57, with 3250 vertices?
math: Decide whether there exists a simple graph $G$ on $3250$ vertices that is $57$-regular, triangle-free, and in which every two distinct non-adjacent vertices have exactly one common neighbour; equivalently, whether a strongly regular graph with parameters $(3250,57,0,1)$ exists.

title: Sylver coinage: who wins after the opening 16?
credit: Conway (game and prize problem); Berlekamp–Conway–Guy, Winning Ways; Guy (1976); Sicherman (2002)
premise_risks: Appears in Conway's prize list; it is not usually called a named conjecture, but some readers may call it 'Conway's 16 problem'
May reduce to a large but finite computation once the position becomes coprime; but the first stage is infinite-branching
plain: In Sylver coinage two players take turns naming positive integers. You may not name a number that can be written as a sum of numbers already named (repeats allowed), and whoever names 1 loses. Every prime 5 or larger is a winning first move. Any other winning first move must have the form 2^a 3^b, and the openings 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12 are known to lose. Which player wins if the first player opens with 16?
math: A position is a finite set $S\subset\mathbb Z_{>0}$; a legal move from $S$ is any integer $n\ge 2$ not in the additive monoid $\langle S\rangle$, giving $S\cup\{n\}$. Under normal play the player with no legal move loses (this matches the rule that naming $1$ loses). Every play is finite, by Dickson's lemma. Decide whether $\{16\}$ is a $\mathcal P$-position (the player who named $16$ wins) or an $\mathcal N$-position.

title: Maker-Breaker 7-in-a-row on the infinite grid
credit: Positional game folklore; Beck, Combinatorial Games: Tic-Tac-Toe Theory; Hollósi–Pluhár (2021)
premise_risks: Answer could plausibly need a large computer search over strip games
Infinite-board game: formal statement needs strategies on histories
plain: Two players take turns claiming cells of the infinite square grid. Maker wins if she ever owns k consecutive cells in a row, column or diagonal, and Breaker wins if he stops this forever. Maker wins for k <= 5, and Breaker wins for k >= 8 with a pairing strategy. Does Breaker win for k = 7?
math: Maker and Breaker alternately claim one unclaimed cell of $\mathbb Z^2$, Maker first. A winning line is a set $\{p+i d:0\le i<7\}$ with $p\in\mathbb Z^2$ and $d\in\{(1,0),(0,1),(1,1),(1,-1)\}$. Decide whether Breaker has a strategy such that, against every Maker strategy, Maker never owns all cells of any winning line. (The analogous question for $k=6$ is also open.)

title: Does ex(n, K_{4,4}) grow faster than n^{5/3}?
credit: Erdős (question as posed in Chung–Graham's Erdős problems collection); Zarankiewicz problem background
premise_risks: Sits inside the Zarankiewicz problem (person-named); the specific K_{4,4} question is an unnamed sub-question
Very hard; partial progress may come only for K_{4,6} first
plain: How many edges can a graph on n vertices have if it contains no complete bipartite graph K_{4,4}? The general upper bound is of order n^{7/4}. The best known constructions give only order n^{5/3}, which is already achieved by graphs that avoid the smaller K_{3,3}. Can one do better than a constant times n^{5/3}?
math: Let $\mathrm{ex}(n,K_{4,4})$ be the maximum number of edges in a $K_{4,4}$-free graph on $n$ vertices. Known: $c\,n^{5/3}\le\mathrm{ex}(n,K_{4,4})\le C\,n^{7/4}$. Decide whether $\mathrm{ex}(n,K_{4,4})=O(n^{5/3})$, i.e. whether $\limsup_n \mathrm{ex}(n,K_{4,4})/n^{5/3}<\infty$. (Stronger target: $\mathrm{ex}(n,K_{4,4})=\Theta(n^{7/4})$.)

title: Linear arboricity of graphs with maximum degree 7
credit: Akiyama–Exoo–Harary (conjecture); small-case history in Christoph et al. (2025)
premise_risks: Could not verify the content of a c.2023 Georgia State preprint 'A decomposition method on solving the linear arboricity conjecture'; it might treat D=7
The full conjecture is sometimes attributed by name (Akiyama–Exoo–Harary); the D=7 case is an unnamed sub-question
Unchecked: G. Chen (GSU, 2023 preprint) 'A decomposition method on solving the linear arboricity conjecture' may cover degree 7; a 2025 survey (arXiv:2507.20500) still lists degree 7 as open.
plain: A linear forest is a graph whose components are paths. The linear arboricity conjecture says the edges of any graph with maximum degree D can be split into ceil((D+1)/2) linear forests. It was proved for D = 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 by 1988, but D = 7 is the smallest open case. Can the edges of every graph with maximum degree 7 be split into 4 linear forests?
math: Prove or disprove: every finite simple graph $G$ with $\Delta(G)\le 7$ admits a map $c:E(G)\to\{1,2,3,4\}$ such that every colour class is a linear forest (acyclic, with maximum degree at most $2$). Equivalently, $\mathrm{la}(G)\le 4$ whenever $\Delta(G)\le 7$.

title: The domination game 3/5 bound for all isolate-free graphs
credit: Kinnersley, West and Zamani (2013); Brešar, Klavžar and Rall (domination game)
premise_risks: Is the full '3/5-conjecture' (named by a fraction, not a person)
Forest case rests partly on an unrefereed long preprint; irrelevant to the general claim
plain: In the domination game on a graph, Dominator and Staller take turns choosing vertices. Each chosen vertex must dominate (be, or be adjacent to) at least one vertex not yet dominated, and the game ends when every vertex is dominated. Dominator wants the game to be short and Staller wants it long. With Dominator moving first and optimal play, does the game always end within 3n/5 moves on an n-vertex graph with no isolated vertices?
math: For a finite graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with no isolated vertex, let $\gamma_g(G)$ be the number of moves under optimal play: players alternately choose a vertex $v$ with $N[v]\not\subseteq N[S]$, where $S$ is the set of vertices chosen so far; Dominator moves first and minimizes the length, Staller maximizes it, and the game ends when $N[S]=V(G)$. Prove or disprove $\gamma_g(G)\le 3n/5$. Best known: $\gamma_g(G)\le 5n/8$.

title: Threshold bias of the Maker-Breaker triangle game
credit: Chvátal and Erdős (1978); Balogh–Samotij; Glazik–Srivastav
premise_risks: The game is often called the 'Chvátal–Erdős triangle game' (person-named object), but the constant question is not a named conjecture
'Improve either bound' form: both directions are hard, but scorer may prefer exact determination
Supporting 2026 budget-variant result is an unrefereed preprint (context only)
plain: On the edges of the complete graph K_n, Maker claims one edge per turn and Breaker claims q edges per turn; Maker wins if she ever owns a triangle. Let q_0(n) be the smallest q for which Breaker wins. It is known that q_0(n) lies between about 1.414 sqrt(n) and 1.633 sqrt(n). What is the right constant, conjecturally sqrt(2)? As a concrete step, can either bound be improved by a constant factor?
math: Let $q_0(n)$ be the least $q$ such that Breaker wins the $(1:q)$ Maker-Breaker triangle game on $E(K_n)$ (Maker first). Known: $(\sqrt2-o(1))\sqrt n\le q_0(n)\le(\sqrt{8/3}+o(1))\sqrt n$. Prove that one of the two bounds can be improved by a constant factor: either there is $c'<\sqrt{8/3}$ with $q_0(n)\le c'\sqrt n$ for all large $n$, or there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $q_0(n)\ge(\sqrt2+\varepsilon)\sqrt n$ for all large $n$.

title: Separating words below the cube-root barrier
credit: Goralčík and Koubek (1986) posed the problem; Robson (1989); Chase (2021).
premise_risks: The withdrawn 2025 O(log^2 n) claim; confirm no revived version.
The 2026 refinement (2609.08191) and 'Further remarks' (2608.30928) are unrefereed but do not affect the target.
plain: Given two different binary words of the same length n, how small a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is needed to accept one and reject the other? The best known upper bound is about n^{1/3} states and the best lower bound is only about log n. Prove that O(n^c) states always suffice for some exponent c < 1/3.
math: For distinct $u,v\in\{0,1\}^n$ let $\mathrm{sep}(u,v)$ be the least number of states of a DFA over $\{0,1\}$ that accepts exactly one of $u,v$, and let $S(n)=\max\{\mathrm{sep}(u,v):u\ne v,\ |u|=|v|=n\}$. Prove that there exist $c<1/3$ and $C>0$ with $S(n)\le C\,n^{c}$ for all $n\ge2$. (Known: $\Omega(\log n)\le S(n)\le O(n^{1/3}\log^{7}n)$; the conjectured truth is $S(n)=O(\log n)$.)

title: A subcubic bound for reset words
credit: Unnamed weakening of the Černý conjecture; bounds by Pin, Frankl, Szykuła, Shitov.
premise_risks: Must ensure no 2026 preprint claims a subcubic or quadratic general bound (none found).
Some may view it as a famous problem in disguise, but it is a strictly weaker, separately-stated open question.
plain: A finite automaton is synchronizing if some input word sends every state to one and the same state; the shortest such word is called a reset word. For automata with n states the shortest reset word is conjectured to have length at most (n-1)^2, but the best proven bound is still about n^3/6. Prove any bound that is asymptotically smaller than n^3.
math: For a complete DFA $\mathcal A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta)$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, call $w\in\Sigma^*$ reset if $|\delta(Q,w)|=1$; let $\mathrm{rt}(\mathcal A)$ be the length of a shortest reset word, and $C(n)=\max\{\mathrm{rt}(\mathcal A): |Q|=n,\ \mathcal A\text{ synchronizing},\ \Sigma\text{ finite}\}$ (finite, since $\mathrm{rt}(\mathcal A)<2^n$). Prove $C(n)=o(n^3)$. (Known: $(n-1)^2\le C(n)\le(7/48+15625/798768)\,n^3+o(n^3)\approx0.1654\,n^3$.)

title: A regular language of generalized star height two
credit: Classical problem (Eggan 1963 for ordinary star height; generalized version promoted by Brzozowski, Pin, Straubing, Thérien).
premise_risks: The OpenAI <=3 bounds (Sept 2026) are unrefereed; they are context, not premises.
The statement is well known (low novelty) but not on the board.
plain: Regular expressions built from letters using union, concatenation, complement and Kleene star describe exactly the regular languages. The generalized star height of a language is the smallest nesting depth of stars any such expression needs. Languages that need zero stars (the star-free ones) and languages that need one star (like (aa)*) are known, but nobody knows whether any regular language needs two. Decide whether every regular language has generalized star height at most one.
math: Generalized regular expressions over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ are built from $\emptyset,\{\varepsilon\},a\ (a\in\Sigma)$ by $E\cup F$, $EF$, $\Sigma^*\setminus E$ and $E^*$, with height $h(E^*)=1+h(E)$, $h$ of atoms $=0$, and $h$ of the other operations the maximum of the arguments' heights. For regular $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ let $h_\Sigma(L)=\min\{h(E):\mathcal L(E)=L\}$. Decide whether there exist a finite $\Sigma$ and a regular $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ with $h_\Sigma(L)\ge2$; equivalently, whether $h_\Sigma(L)\le1$ for every regular $L$. Either answer solves the problem.
review_note: Context (AI-lab announcement, treated as correct): OpenAI 134: Generalized star height at most three. Every regular language has generalized star height <=3, so the uniform-boundedness question is settled. The board question (does any L have height >=2, i.e. is the maximum 1 or in {2,3}) is still open. Update the known-bounds context.

title: Two colours, sums of at most two: does every solution compute the halting problem?
credit: Hindman–Leader–Strauss (2003) question; Dzhafarov, Jockusch, Solomon, Westrick; Carlucci, Kołodziejczyk, Lepore, Zdanowski.
premise_risks: The computable formulation is slightly different from the RCA0 implication; a positive answer that relativizes gives HT^{<=2}_2 -> ACA0, a negative answer alone does not separate them.
Check Bompard–Liu–Patey and any 2025-2026 work for an unpublicized resolution.
plain: Hindman's theorem says that for any finite colouring of the positive integers there is an infinite set H all of whose finite sums have one colour. Restrict this to sums of one or two distinct elements. A computable 4-colouring is known to force every such H to compute the halting problem, but with only 2 colours (and no extra 'apartness' condition) nobody knows. Decide whether some computable 2-colouring forces every solution to compute the halting problem.
math: For $H\subseteq\mathbb N_{>0}$ let $FS^{\le2}(H)=H\cup\{x+y:x,y\in H,\ x\ne y\}$. Decide whether there exists a computable $c:\mathbb N_{>0}\to\{0,1\}$ such that every infinite $H\subseteq\mathbb N_{>0}$ on which $FS^{\le2}(H)$ is $c$-monochromatic satisfies $\emptyset'\le_T H$. Either answer is a solution. (A relativizable positive answer gives $\mathsf{RCA}_0\vdash\mathsf{HT}^{\le2}_2\to\mathsf{ACA}_0$.)

title: Only 2^{O(n^2)} triangulated 3-spheres on n vertices?
credit: Gap stated by Kalai (1988), Pfeifle–Ziegler (2004), Nevo–Wilson (2013), Nevo–Santos–Wilson (2016).
premise_risks: Closing this specific log factor is a natural open gap but not singled out as a numbered open problem in the sources; Nevo–Santos–Wilson call their lower bound 'close to' the upper bound.
Durhuus–Pavelka (Nov 2026) is unrefereed; used only for context on the facet version.
plain: Count the triangulations of the 3-dimensional sphere on n labelled vertices. Constructions give at least 2^{cn^2} of them, while the only upper bound, from counting all possible sets of tetrahedra, is 2^{Cn^2 log n}. Decide which is the truth: is the count at most 2^{Cn^2}, or does the log n factor really occur?
math: Let $s(n)$ be the number of simplicial complexes $K$ on vertex set $[n]$ (every vertex used) with $|K|\cong S^3$. Known: $2^{\Omega(n^2)}\le s(n)\le 2^{O(n^2\log n)}$. Decide whether $\log_2 s(n)=O(n^2)$ (i.e. $\exists C\ \forall n:\ s(n)\le 2^{Cn^2}$) or $\log_2 s(n)/n^2\to\infty$ along some subsequence.

title: The centred maximal function diminishes variation
credit: Question raised in the regularity-of-maximal-functions literature (Aldaz-Perez Lazaro; Kurka 2015; Carneiro survey 2019); not a named conjecture.
premise_risks: Continuous/discrete equivalence is proved in 2407.06734 only for the step-function class; state both versions explicitly rather than claiming equivalence in general
Var(f) must be the essential (normalized) variation in the continuous version
plain: Replace a function on the real line by its centred maximal average: at each point take the largest average of |f| over intervals centred there. The total variation of the new function should be no larger than that of f. This is known for the uncentred maximal function and, for the centred one, for indicator functions and special step functions; for general f the best proven bound allows growth by a factor 240,004.
math: For locally integrable $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ let $Mf(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac{1}{2r}\int_{x-r}^{x+r}|f(y)|\,dy$. Prove or disprove: for every $f$ of bounded variation, $\operatorname{Var}(Mf)\le\operatorname{Var}(f)$, where $\operatorname{Var}(f)$ is the essential variation (variation of the best normalized representative) and $\operatorname{Var}(Mf)$ is the pointwise variation of the everywhere-defined function $Mf$. Discrete companion (also open; a separate statement, not part of the main claim): for finitely supported $f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $Mf(n)=\sup_{r\in\mathbb{N}_0}\frac{1}{2r+1}\sum_{|k|\le r}|f(n+k)|$, prove $\sum_{n}|Mf(n+1)-Mf(n)|\le\sum_n|f(n+1)-f(n)|$. The constant 1 cannot be improved.

title: Sign uncertainty on the line: reach 1/2
credit: Bourgain-Clozel-Kahane sign uncertainty constant; target 1/2 chosen as first value beyond reach of the 2017 rearrangement method (QED framing).
premise_risks: Threshold 1/2 is a round-number choice, justified only by the 2017 authors' remark that the method yields only third-decimal gains
Upper bound 0.5671 is from an unrefereed AI-search report; refereed upper bound is 0.594
Literature sometimes states the result for A(f)A(f̂) (product) vs its square root; keep the product form 1/4
plain: If a real even function f on the line has f(0) ≤ 0 and its Fourier transform is also ≤ 0 at the origin, then f and its transform cannot both become permanently nonnegative too soon: with A(f), A(f̂) the radii beyond which each is nonnegative, the product A(f)A(f̂) is bounded below. The best proven lower bound for the square root of this product is 0.45 (2017), while the best examples give about 0.567. Prove the bound 1/2.
math: With $\hat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}dx$, let $\mathcal{A}_+$ be the set of nonzero real-valued even continuous $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ with $\hat f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$, $f(0)\le0$, $\hat f(0)\le0$, and $f,\hat f$ eventually nonnegative; for real $g$ put $A(g)=\inf\{r>0: g(x)\ge0\text{ for all }|x|\ge r\}$. Prove $A(f)A(\hat f)\ge 1/4$ for all $f\in\mathcal{A}_+$, i.e. $\mathbb{A}_+(1):=\inf_{f\in\mathcal A_+}\sqrt{A(f)A(\hat f)}\ge 1/2$ (currently $0.45\le\mathbb{A}_+(1)\le 0.5671$).

title: Optimal sphere packing in dimension 4
credit: Classical; Conway–Sloane
premise_risks: Unrefereed 2026 claimed proofs (preprints.org 202606.0856; arXiv:2609.25120) — verify status
plain: What is the densest way to pack equal balls in 4-dimensional space? The D4 lattice packing (density π²/16) is believed optimal and has been known to be the best lattice packing since 1873, but denser non-lattice packings have never been ruled out. Prove that no packing beats π²/16.
math: Let $\Delta_4$ be the supremum, over all packings of congruent open balls in $\mathbb{R}^4$, of the upper density $\limsup_{R\to\infty}\mathrm{vol}(\bigcup B\cap B(0,R))/\mathrm{vol}(B(0,R))$. Prove $\Delta_4=\pi^2/16$, the density of the $D_4$ lattice packing.

title: Optimal sphere packing in dimension 5, 6 or 7
credit: Classical
plain: In dimensions 5, 6 and 7 the densest known ball packings come from the lattices D5, E6 and E7, which are known to be the best lattice packings. Prove that at least one of them is optimal among all packings.
math: Let $\Delta_n$ be the supremum of upper densities of packings of congruent balls in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Prove that at least one of $\Delta_5=\pi^2/(15\sqrt2)$ (density of $D_5$), $\Delta_6=\pi^3/(48\sqrt3)$ (density of $E_6$), $\Delta_7=\pi^3/105$ (density of $E_7$) holds.

title: Beat (3+√2)/2 for diamond-free families
credit: Problem line from Griggs–Lu and Griggs–Li–Lu. Upper bound (3+√2)/2 by Grósz, Methuku, Tompkins (2018). Lower bound 2.1479 by Tompkins (2026). Three-layer bound by Balogh, Hu, Lidický, Liu.
premise_risks: The lower bound 2.1479 (and the disproof of the diamond conjecture) rests on an unrefereed July 2026 preprint (arXiv:2607.09497). The Claim itself does not depend on it.
The Ai–Liu–Song window-density results are an unrefereed 2026 preprint.
An improved upper bound might exist in a recent preprint not indexed by search.
plain: A family of subsets of {1,...,n} is diamond-free if it contains no four distinct sets A, B, C, D with A ⊂ B ⊂ D and A ⊂ C ⊂ D. For years it was believed that the two middle layers, about 2·binom(n, n/2) sets, are optimal; in July 2026 a random linear-algebra construction beat that with about 2.1479·binom(n, n/2) sets. The best general upper bound, (3+√2)/2 ≈ 2.2071 times binom(n, n/2), dates from 2016–2018. Lower it by any fixed amount.
math: Let $La(n,Q_2)$ be the maximum size of $\mathcal F\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ containing no four distinct $A,B,C,D\in\mathcal F$ with $A\subsetneq B\subsetneq D$ and $A\subsetneq C\subsetneq D$. Prove that $\limsup_{n\to\infty} La(n,Q_2)/\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} < \frac{3+\sqrt2}{2}$. (Known: $\liminf \ge 2+\frac{29}{135}\prod_{i\ge1}(1-4^{-i})\approx 2.1479$; for families inside three consecutive middle layers the density is at most $2.15121$. Stretch goal: determine the limit, whose existence is itself unknown.)

title: Turán density of the tight 5-cycle
credit: Conjectured value from the Mubayi–Rödl construction (the conjecture is usually attributed to them, but the problem is not person-named). Upper bound by Razborov. Related progress by Kamčev, Letzter, Pokrovskiy and the authors of arXiv:2506.03223.
premise_risks: The conjecture is sometimes informally attributed to Mubayi and Rödl, which is a mild naming risk. It is normally stated simply as 'π(C_5^3) = 2√3 − 3'.
The best upper bound might have been sharpened slightly by unpublished flag-algebra runs (for example 0.4683 vs 0.468). This does not affect the target.
plain: A 3-uniform hypergraph is a collection of triples of points. The tight 5-cycle consists of five points v0,...,v4 arranged in a circle together with the five triples of cyclically consecutive points. What is the largest fraction of all triples a hypergraph on n points can contain without a tight 5-cycle, as n grows? An iterated construction achieves 2√3 − 3 ≈ 0.4641, and flag algebras give an upper bound of about 0.468. Prove that 2√3 − 3 is the answer.
math: For a 3-graph $H$ write $C_5^{(3)}\subseteq H$ if there are distinct $v_0,\dots,v_4\in V(H)$ with $\{v_i,v_{i+1},v_{i+2}\}\in E(H)$ for all $i\in\mathbb Z/5$. Let $\mathrm{ex}(n)=\max\{|E(H)|: |V(H)|=n,\ C_5^{(3)}\not\subseteq H\}$. Prove that $\pi(C_5^{(3)}):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{ex}(n)/\binom n3 = 2\sqrt3-3$. (The limit exists by averaging; $\pi(C_5^{(3)})\ge 2\sqrt3-3$ is known.)

title: Property B: beat the square-root exponent
credit: Classical problem (Property B, named for F. Bernstein's property; studied by Erdős and Hajnal). Bounds by Erdős, Beck, Radhakrishnan–Srinivasan, Cherkashin–Kozik.
premise_risks: 'Property B' is named after Bernstein (object name, not a named conjecture). It is sometimes called 'the Erdős–Hajnal property B problem', which is a mild naming risk.
A well-known classical problem, so novelty is low.
plain: Let m(n) be the fewest sets of size n needed so that however you colour the points red and blue, some set is entirely one colour. A random construction shows m(n) is at most about n²·2ⁿ. The best lower bound, from 2000, is about √(n/log n)·2ⁿ. The task is to show that m(n) is at least n^{1/2+δ}·2ⁿ for some fixed δ > 0, a polynomial improvement over the square-root barrier.
math: Let $m(n)$ be the minimum number of edges of an $n$-uniform hypergraph that is not 2-colourable (has no vertex 2-colouring without a monochromatic edge). Prove there exist $\delta>0$ and $c>0$ such that $m(n)\ge c\,n^{1/2+\delta}\,2^n$ for all $n\ge1$.

title: Does a perfect cuboid exist?
credit: Classical (Euler; Kraitchik; listed as D18 in Guy, Unsolved Problems in Number Theory).
premise_risks: Several unrefereed 2026 nonexistence claims (arXiv:2602.00239 math.GM, arXiv:2604.28072) exist; none accepted, but the scorer should know they are out there
Very famous: low novelty
plain: Is there a box whose three edges, three face diagonals and space diagonal all have whole-number lengths? Boxes with whole-number edges and face diagonals (Euler bricks, such as 44 × 117 × 240) come in infinite families, but in every known one the space diagonal is irrational. Nobody has found a perfect box or proved that none exists.
math: Decide whether there exist positive integers $a,b,c$ such that $a^2+b^2$, $b^2+c^2$, $c^2+a^2$ and $a^2+b^2+c^2$ are all perfect squares.

title: A 3×3 magic square of distinct squares
credit: LaBar (College Math. J. 1984); Gardner (Quantum 1996); Guy UPINT D15.
premise_risks: Unrefereed nonexistence claim arXiv:2510.08286 (not accepted)
Famous recreational problem: novelty moderate
plain: Can nine different perfect squares be arranged in a 3×3 grid so that every row, every column and both diagonals have the same sum? Such squares exist in size 4×4 and larger, and 3×3 examples with seven square entries are known, but no full 3×3 example has been found and none has been ruled out.
math: Decide whether there exist integers $x_{ij}$ ($1\le i,j\le 3$) such that the nine numbers $x_{ij}^2$ are pairwise distinct and the matrix $(x_{ij}^2)$ is magic: its three row sums, three column sums and two diagonal sums are all equal.

title: Infinitely many non-Wieferich primes
credit: Folklore; Silverman (1988) conditional proof; Guy UPINT A3.
premise_risks: Very well-known; novelty modest
Must not be confused with the (also open) question of infinitely many Wieferich primes
plain: By Fermat's little theorem, every odd prime p divides 2^(p−1)−1. Usually p^2 does not; the only known exceptions are 1093 and 3511, and there are none other below 2^64. Yet nobody can prove that the usual case happens infinitely often: are there infinitely many primes p with p^2 not dividing 2^(p−1)−1?
math: Prove that the set $\{p\text{ prime}: 2^{p-1}\not\equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}\}$ is infinite.

title: Does the odd greedy algorithm always terminate?
credit: Stein, Selfridge, Graham (via Guy UPINT; Klee–Wagon 1991); erdosproblems.com #282.
premise_risks: Appears on erdosproblems.com; not itself person-named, but the owner may count 'Erdős problem #282' as person-attributed
May be considered a 'Collatz-type' problem with little available theory
plain: Every fraction with an odd denominator can be written as a sum of distinct unit fractions with odd denominators. The odd greedy algorithm tries to find such a sum by repeatedly subtracting the largest unit fraction 1/n, with n odd, that still fits. Does it always stop after finitely many steps when the starting fraction has an odd denominator? In every case tested it does, sometimes only after surprisingly many steps.
math: For $x\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)$ with odd denominator, set $x_0=x$. While $x_k>0$, let $n_k$ be the least odd integer with $1/n_k\le x_k$ and set $x_{k+1}=x_k-1/n_k$. Prove or disprove: for every such $x$ there is a $k$ with $x_k=0$.

title: A point at rational distance from all four corners of a square
credit: Classical; Guy UPINT D19; Berry (1990); Bremner–Guy.
premise_risks: May be judged geometry rather than number theory (it is a Diophantine problem)
Famous recreational problem; moderate novelty
plain: Is there a point in the plane whose distances to all four corners of the unit square are rational numbers? Points at rational distance from three of the corners are dense in the plane, but no point has been found that also works for the fourth corner, and no one has shown that none exists.
math: Decide whether there exist $x,y\in\mathbb R$ such that $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, $\sqrt{(x-1)^2+y^2}$, $\sqrt{x^2+(y-1)^2}$ and $\sqrt{(x-1)^2+(y-1)^2}$ are all rational. (Any such $x,y$ are automatically rational.)

title: An odd weird number
credit: Benkoski and Erdős (1974); erdosproblems.com #470.
premise_risks: Attributed as an Erdős problem (#470); the question itself is not person-named
Abundancy-cap context uses an unrefereed 2026 preprint
Already formalized in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (helpful, but shows it is well known)
plain: A number is abundant if its proper divisors add up to more than the number itself, and weird if it is abundant but no selection of its distinct proper divisors adds up to exactly the number (70 is the smallest). Weird numbers have positive density, but every known one is even. Does an odd weird number exist?
math: Decide whether there exists an odd $n\in\mathbb N$ with $\sigma(n)>2n$ such that no subset $S$ of the proper divisors of $n$ satisfies $\sum_{d\in S}d=n$.

title: Three mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order 10
credit: Classical. Recent work by Myrvold, McKay–Meynert–Myrvold, and the 2026 SAT study arXiv:2503.10504
premise_risks: A massive SAT/computer search could settle it at any time (SAT groups are actively working on it)
Low novelty: very well known
plain: Two Latin squares of the same size are orthogonal if, when you lay one on top of the other, every ordered pair of symbols appears exactly once. Euler's 36-officers problem shows no orthogonal pair exists for order 6, but orthogonal pairs of order 10 were found in 1959. Nobody knows whether three Latin squares of order 10 can be pairwise orthogonal.
math: Let $N(n)$ be the maximum number of pairwise orthogonal Latin squares of order $n$. Decide whether $N(10)\ge 3$, i.e. whether there exist $L_1,L_2,L_3:[10]\times[10]\to[10]$, each a Latin square, such that for every $a\ne b$ the map $(i,j)\mapsto (L_a(i,j),L_b(i,j))$ is a bijection $[10]^2\to[10]^2$.

title: Does a projective plane of order 12 exist?
credit: Classical (Veblen–Bussey era question). Partial results by Janko, van Trung and others.
premise_risks: Very well known, so novelty is low
May be judged a 'famous problem' (the prime power conjecture for planes), but the specific order-12 case is the natural unnamed sub-question
Overlaps thematically with MOLS(10) (both are MOLS questions); the owner may want only one
plain: A finite projective plane of order n has n^2+n+1 points and the same number of lines. Every line has n+1 points, and any two points lie on exactly one common line. Planes exist whenever n is a prime power, they are impossible for n = 6 and n = 10, and no plane is known for any other n. The smallest unsettled order is 12.
math: Decide whether there exists a finite incidence structure with $157$ points and $157$ lines in which every line contains exactly $13$ points, every point lies on exactly $13$ lines, and any two distinct points lie on exactly one common line. Equivalently: is there a $157\times157$ $0/1$ matrix $A$ with $AA^{\mathsf T}=12I+J$, or equivalently are there $11$ mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order $12$?

title: Every non-abelian p-group has a non-inner automorphism of order p
credit: Y. Berkovich (Kourovka Notebook Problem 4.13); survey by Sarkar–Joshi
premise_risks: Naming: usually called the 'non-inner automorphism conjecture', but some papers call it 'Berkovich's conjecture'. The owner may treat it as person-named.
Possible incremental partial results in 2025-26 that I did not find; no resolution claim found
plain: Every group acts on itself by conjugation, and these 'inner' automorphisms are its obvious symmetries. Does every finite non-abelian group whose order is a power of a prime p have an automorphism that is not inner and that gives the identity when applied p times? Gaschütz proved in 1966 that a non-inner automorphism of p-power order always exists, but getting order exactly p has resisted proof for decades.
math: For every prime $p$ and every finite non-abelian $p$-group $G$, prove that there exists $\varphi\in\mathrm{Aut}(G)\setminus\mathrm{Inn}(G)$ with $\varphi^p=\mathrm{id}$ (such a $\varphi$ has order exactly $p$), or find a counterexample.

title: No perfect single-error-correcting code over a 6-letter alphabet
credit: Folklore conjecture on perfect codes over non-prime-power alphabets; Golomb–Posner, Heden–Roos, Heden's survey
premise_risks: Exact list of excluded lengths for q=6 not fully verified (some other paper might exclude 43); does not affect the general claim
Heden–Roos 2011 citation details from secondary source
plain: A code of words of length n over a 6-letter alphabet is 1-perfect if every possible word is either a codeword or differs from exactly one codeword in exactly one position. Over alphabets whose size is a prime power, such codes (Hamming codes) exist in infinitely many lengths. Over 6 letters none is known for n≥2. Counting arguments and Lloyd's theorem leave only lengths 7, 19, 43, 97, 115, 259, ..., and only 7 and 19 have been ruled out. Prove that none exists.
math: Let $H(n,6)=\{0,\dots,5\}^n$ with the Hamming distance $d$. Prove that for no $n\ge2$ is there $C\subseteq H(n,6)$ such that every $x\in H(n,6)$ has exactly one $c\in C$ with $d(x,c)\le1$. (Necessary conditions: $1+5n=2^a3^b$ and, by Lloyd's theorem, $6\mid 1+5n$, so $n\in\{7,19,43,97,115,259,\dots\}$. The cases $n=7$ (Golomb\u2013Posner) and $n=19$ (Heden\u2013Roos) are excluded.)

title: Eight points with integer distances in general position
credit: Question posed by Kreisel and Kurz (2008), in the line of Erdos's question on integral point sets in general position
premise_risks: Could be resolved by a large computer search (it is a recognised open problem with refereed literature, but a positive answer might be pure computation)
Erdos's broader question is attributed to a person, but this specific 8-point question is unnamed
plain: Can you place eight points in the plane so that every pair is an integer distance apart, no three points lie on a line, and no four lie on a circle? Seven such points were found by computer in 2008. Nobody has found eight or shown that eight is impossible.
math: Decide whether there exist pairwise distinct $p_1,\dots,p_8\in\mathbb{R}^2$ such that $|p_i-p_j|\in\mathbb{Z}$ for all $i,j$, no three of the $p_i$ are collinear, and no four of the $p_i$ are concyclic.

title: How many faces can a convex space-filler have?
credit: Grunbaum and Shephard, 'Tilings with congruent tiles', Bull. AMS 1980, Problem (G)
premise_risks: The 54-faced Wolfram 'space-filling polyhedron' must be confirmed non-convex (if convex and genuine it would only beat the record, not settle boundedness)
Possible unlocated progress in crystallographic literature on non-isohedral convex tiles
plain: A convex polyhedron is a space-filler if congruent copies of it fill all of 3-space with no gaps or overlaps. In the plane a convex tile has at most 6 sides, but in space the record is 38 faces (Engel, 1981). Is there any finite upper bound at all on the number of faces of a convex space-filler?
math: Call a convex polytope $P\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ with nonempty interior a monohedral prototile if there are isometries $g_1,g_2,\dots$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with $\bigcup_i g_iP=\mathbb{R}^3$ and $\operatorname{int}(g_iP)\cap\operatorname{int}(g_jP)=\emptyset$ for $i\neq j$ (the tiling need not be face-to-face, isohedral or periodic). Decide whether there is $N<\infty$ such that every monohedral prototile in $\mathbb{R}^3$ has at most $N$ facets.

title: Largest lattice 4-polytope with one interior lattice point
