credit: Conjecture 1.7 in Nill's paper on reflexive simplices; proved for simplices and the reflexive case (Balletti–Kasprzyk–Nill, Forum Math. Sigma 2022, arXiv:1611.02455); the extremal simplex is due to Zaks–Perles–Wills.
premise_risks: Extremal simplex is called the Zaks-Perles-Wills simplex (object name, allowed); the conjecture itself is not person-named
Uniqueness is irrelevant to the bound; in d=3 the bound is attained by more than one polytope, so check claims of uniqueness separately
plain: Take a polytope in 4-dimensional space whose corners all have integer coordinates and which contains exactly one integer point in its interior. How large can its volume be? The best known example is the simplex with vertices 0, 2e1, 3e2, 7e3, 84e4, of volume 147, and it is known to be the largest among simplices. Is it the largest among all such polytopes?
math: Let $P=\operatorname{conv}(V)\subset\mathbb{R}^4$ with $V\subset\mathbb{Z}^4$ finite and $|\operatorname{int}(P)\cap\mathbb{Z}^4|=1$. Prove that $\operatorname{vol}_4(P)\le 147=\tfrac{2(s_4-1)^2}{4!}$, where $s_1=2,s_2=3,s_3=7,s_4=43$ are the Sylvester numbers. Equality holds for $\operatorname{conv}(0,2e_1,3e_2,7e_3,84e_4)$. (Here vol is Euclidean volume, so normalized volume is $3528$. The same bound $2(s_d-1)^2/d!$ is conjectured for every $d\ge4$.)

title: Every centrally symmetric 5-polytope has at least 243 faces
credit: Kalai (1989); d = 4 case Sanyal-Werner-Ziegler (2009)
premise_risks: Sub-case of a person-named conjecture (allowed by rules as an unnamed dimension-specific sub-question)
Google DeepMind formal-conjectures may already host a formal statement (helps formalization, but signals visibility)
plain: A polytope is centrally symmetric if it looks the same after reflection through its centre, like a cube or an octahedron. The 5-dimensional cube has 3^5 = 243 non-empty faces (counting the polytope itself), and so does the 5-dimensional cross-polytope. It is conjectured that no centrally symmetric 5-polytope has fewer. This is proved in dimensions up to 4 and open in dimension 5.
math: Let $P\subset\mathbb R^5$ be a full-dimensional convex polytope with $P=-P$. Prove that $P$ has at least $3^5=243$ non-empty faces, where the faces are the sets $\{x\in P:\langle a,x\rangle=\max_{y\in P}\langle a,y\rangle\}$, $a\in\mathbb R^5$ ($a=0$ gives $P$ itself).

title: Beat n^2 empty triangles
credit: Problem of determining h_3(n) asymptotically (Barany, Valtr and others); bounds by Katchalski-Meir, Dumitrescu, Garcia, Aichholzer et al., Barany-Valtr
premise_risks: An unpublished or less visible improvement of the n^2 lower bound may exist (searches found none)
Lower bound attributions (Dumitrescu 2000, Garcia 2012) recalled from secondary sources; the 2014 bound is confirmed
plain: Scatter n points in the plane with no three on a line. A triangle with corners among the points is empty if no other point is inside it. Every such configuration has at least about n^2 empty triangles, and the best constructions have about 1.62 n^2. Show that every configuration actually has at least (1+c) n^2 empty triangles for some fixed c > 0.
math: For a finite $S\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ with no three points collinear, let $e(S)$ be the number of 3-subsets $T\subseteq S$ with $\operatorname{conv}(T)\cap S=T$. Let $h_3(n)=\min_{|S|=n}e(S)$. Prove that there is $c>0$ with $h_3(n)\ge(1+c)\,n^2$ for all sufficiently large $n$. (Known: $n^2-\tfrac{32}{7}n+\tfrac{22}{7}\le h_3(n)\le(1.6195\ldots+o(1))\,n^2$.)

title: Rational 6-cycles of z^2+c
credit: Stoll (2008); open case of the Morton-Silverman / Flynn-Poonen-Schaefer programme
premise_risks: The full statement 'no period > 3' is the named Flynn-Poonen-Schaefer conjecture. This candidate is only its unnamed period-6 case, which the naming rule allows.
An unconditional rank computation for J_1(6) could be within reach of modern class-group methods (as in Fu-Stoll 2024), so difficulty may be lower than it looks.
plain: Iterate the map x ↦ x² + c with c and the starting point x rational. A rational starting point can return to itself after exactly 1, 2 or 3 steps (for example c = −29/16, x = −1/4 gives a 3-cycle), and it is proved that exact periods 4 and 5 are impossible. Show, without assuming unproved conjectures, that exact period 6 is impossible too.
math: Prove that there are no $c,x\in\mathbb{Q}$ such that $x$ has exact (minimal) period $6$ under $f_c(z)=z^2+c$.

title: Does the classical Hénon map have a periodic sink?
credit: Hénon (1976); open question as framed by Galias & Tucker (2015)
premise_risks: A positive answer could come from a pure computer search (a certified long-period sink). That is a legitimate solution, but some reviewers may see it as computational.
A negative answer is far beyond current techniques, so the problem may sit open for a long time either way.
plain: The Hénon map H(x,y) = (1 − 1.4x² + y, 0.3x) is the textbook example of a 'strange attractor': on a computer screen its orbits trace out a fractal set. No one has proved that what we see is not just a stable periodic orbit with a very long period. Decide whether H has an attracting periodic orbit.
math: Let $H(x,y)=(1-\tfrac{7}{5}x^2+y,\ \tfrac{3}{10}x)$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$. Decide whether there exist $n\ge1$ and $p\in\mathbb{R}^2$ with $H^n(p)=p$ such that both eigenvalues of $DH^n(p)$ have modulus $<1$.

title: Area of the boundary of the Mandelbrot set
credit: Classical (Milnor's problem lists; Douady-Hubbard era)
premise_risks: Famous and probably very hard (low novelty). It is listed because it is important and has a one-line Lean statement.
It should be checked against the scorer's view of whether it duplicates the existing hyperbolic-measure item QED-M051. It does not: that item asks about the computability of a real-line measure.
plain: The Mandelbrot set M is the set of complex numbers c for which the orbit of 0 under z -> z^2 + c stays bounded. Its boundary is a fractal of Hausdorff dimension 2, as large as possible for a plane set. Does the boundary of M have zero area?
math: Let $M=\{c\in\mathbb C:\sup_n|f_c^{n}(0)|<\infty\}$ with $f_c(z)=z^2+c$. Decide whether the two-dimensional Lebesgue measure of $\partial M$ is $0$.

title: Are the fractional parts of (3/2)^n dense?
credit: Classical (Vijayaraghavan, Mahler, Flatto-Lagarias-Pollington)
premise_risks: Area is borderline: this is uniform distribution / Diophantine analysis rather than core dynamics.
Famous and extremely hard (low novelty). It should not be confused with the named Mahler Z-number problem, which is related but separate.
plain: Write down 3/2, 9/4, 27/8, ... and keep only the part after the decimal point. Numerically these fractional parts look uniformly spread over [0,1), but nobody can prove they even come arbitrarily close to every number in [0,1]. Prove that they do.
math: Prove that $\{ \{(3/2)^n\} : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$ is dense in $[0,1]$, where $\{t\} = t - \lfloor t \rfloor$.

title: Is Euler's constant irrational?
credit: Classical (Euler, Mascheroni)
premise_risks: Very famous and probably out of reach (novelty low). It is included because its importance is high and its formal statement is trivial.
The OpenAI batch claims Catalan's constant irrational. If the same method extends to γ, a claim may appear soon, so recheck before posting.
plain: Euler's constant γ ≈ 0.5772 is the limit of 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n − ln n. It also equals −Γ'(1), where Γ is the Gamma function. More than 280 years after Euler, nobody knows whether γ is a fraction. Prove that it is not.
math: Prove that $\gamma=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\sum_{k=1}^n \tfrac1k-\ln n\right)\notin\mathbb{Q}$.

title: Can additive squares be avoided over the integers?
credit: T. C. Brown and A. R. Freedman (1987); G. Pirillo and S. Varricchio (1994); see also Halbeisen-Hungerbühler, Cassaigne-Currie-Schaeffer-Shallit.
premise_risks: Zhang 2026 preprint (arXiv:2610.02215) is unrefereed but only cited as context
The problem is sometimes informally attributed to its askers, but it is not a person-named conjecture
plain: An additive square in a sequence of integers is a block of 2k consecutive terms whose first half and second half have the same sum (for example 1 3 | 2 2). Is there a finite set of integers S and an infinite sequence with all terms in S that contains no additive square? Such sequences exist over a finite subset of the plane lattice Z², and over Z one can avoid additive cubes (three adjacent blocks of equal length and equal sum), but no one knows whether squares can be avoided over Z.
math: Decide whether there exist a finite set $S\subset\mathbb{Z}$ and $w:\mathbb{N}\to S$ such that for all $i\ge0$ and $k\ge1$, $\sum_{j=i}^{i+k-1}w(j)\neq\sum_{j=i+k}^{i+2k-1}w(j)$. Equivalently, by compactness: is there a finite $S\subset\mathbb Z$ for which arbitrarily long finite words over $S$ avoid additive squares?

title: Square-free words from lists of size three
credit: Posed by J. Grytczuk, J. Przybyło and X. Zhu (2011) in the context of nonrepetitive list colouring; see M. Rosenfeld (2022), V. Bui and M. Rosenfeld (2025).
premise_risks: Occasionally referred to as a conjecture of Grytczuk–Przybyło–Zhu; the usual name is 'the Thue choice number of the path is 3' (object named after Thue), so naming rule is likely satisfied but should be checked
plain: Thue showed in 1906 that there is an infinite word over three letters with no square, that is, no block immediately repeated (like 'abab'). Now suppose each position i has its own list A_i of three allowed symbols, chosen by an adversary from an unbounded alphabet. Is there always an infinite square-free word whose i-th letter lies in A_i? Lists of size 4 are known to suffice, and size 3 suffices when all lists are drawn from only four symbols.
math: Claim: for every sequence $(A_i)_{i\ge1}$ of sets $A_i\subseteq\mathbb N$ with $|A_i|=3$, there exists $w:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N$ with $w(i)\in A_i$ for all $i$, such that there are no $i,k\ge1$ with $w(i+j)=w(i+k+j)$ for all $0\le j<k$. (By compactness, this is equivalent to the same statement for every finite length; that is, the Thue choice number of the path is $3$.)

title: Odd plus odd is even
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: The sum of two odd natural numbers is even.
math: For all $a,b\in\mathbb N$, if $a$ and $b$ are odd then $a+b$ is even.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 2 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: n² + n is even
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: For every integer n, the number n² + n is even.
math: For all $n\in\mathbb Z$, $2\mid n^2+n$.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 4 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: Sum of the first n odd numbers
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: Adding up the first n odd numbers 1 + 3 + 5 + … gives n².
math: For all $n$, $\sum_{i<n}(2i+1)=n^2$.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 8 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: Nicomachus: sum of cubes
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: The sum of the first n cubes equals the square of the sum of the first n numbers.
math: For all $n$, $\sum_{i=0}^{n} i^3=\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n} i\right)^2$.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 16 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: Coins of 3 and 5
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: Every whole number from 8 upward can be paid exactly with coins worth 3 and 5.
math: For every $n\ge 8$ there are $a,b\in\mathbb N$ with $n=3a+5b$.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 32 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: Party of six (R(3,3) ≤ 6)
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: Among any six people, some three all know each other or some three are all strangers.
math: Every simple graph on 6 vertices contains a triangle or an independent set of size 3.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 64 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: Erdős–Szekeres monotone subsequences
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: Any list of rs + 1 distinct real numbers has an increasing run of r + 1 of them or a decreasing run of s + 1 of them (not necessarily consecutive).
math: For $f:\{0,\dots,rs\}\to\mathbb R$ injective there is a set of $r+1$ indices on which $f$ is strictly increasing, or a set of $s+1$ indices on which it is strictly decreasing.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 128 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: Dilworth's theorem
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: In any finite partially ordered set, the largest number of pairwise incomparable elements equals the smallest number of chains needed to cover everything.
math: For every finite poset $P$ there are $k$, an antichain of size $k$, and a partition of $P$ into $k$ chains.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 256 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.
